Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Yesterday I rose in my position as the Whip of the government party with a special House responsibility for notifying my members of the time of votes. We had quite an extended discussion in the Chamber about the kind of notice members are required to have for those votes.
There is another issue I would like to raise this morning, along the same vein. For some considerable period of time, and operating with the general consent of the House, shortly after the bells began to ring a clock would appear on our television screens indicating the maximum amount of time that was available for members to arrive in the Chamber prior to the commencement of the vote. This is a very important principle.
All members will know that according to the Standing Orders of the House, it is possible for the Whip of the Official Opposition and the Whip of the government to walk down the aisle and indicate to the Chair that they are ready for the vote, at some point between the commencement of the bells and the maximum amount of time for the bells ring. In this way we can take the vote more quickly.
We did that for particular reasons on two or three occasions. Some members rose subsequently in the Chamber to indicate that they were not happy with us moving more quickly than the clock indicated. In other words, the clock was providing them with information that in their minds was not correct. We have had these arguments expressed in the House.
Later this day, according to the ruling made by the Speaker yesterday, it is very likely that we are going to have a vote. The Speaker has ruled that members have been given adequate notice of a confidence vote on a Friday, a very unusual circumstance. I cannot remember the last time it has happened in my parliamentary career, and I have been here about 11 years. Nevertheless, that is the situation we face today.
What members need to know when those bells begin to ring is whether or not the time remaining before the commencement of the vote will be displayed on the television screen. To overcome some of the problems caused to some of the members, and I may suggest it was a tiny minority which led to a kind of administrative decision to take the clock away, I think we can resolve this matter.
There are two people in this Chamber who have the responsibility to walk down the aisle and indicate to the Chair that we are ready for the vote. One is the Whip of the government party, or the Whip's designate, the other is the Whip of the Official Opposition, or that Whip's designate.
When bells begin to ring, if either one of us approach the Chair and indicate that we are not going to walk down that aisle until the maximum time has expired, then the clock could commence on the television screen and members, with a sense of soreness, would know exactly when the time had expired and when the vote was to occur. I think that operates in the best interests of the whole House.
If the clock does not appear, then members have to be alert to the fact the vote might occur at any moment and that they should move quickly. But if either Whip goes to the Table and says: "It is not my intention to walk down until the maximum time has come," then I suggest the clock could come back up on the screen and members would have the certitude of the time of the vote.
Surely, in a democracy, the most important responsibility we bear in the final analysis on behalf of our constituents is to be present in the Chamber to cast a vote on their behalf. It is the reason why notice provi-

March 23, 1990
Point of Order
sions exist. It is the reason why we have standing orders which give notice of certain kinds of intentions so that members can have a degree of certitude.
We think that the clock added to that certitude. Many members on this side of the House were very unhappy when the clock disappeared, others felt clotheslined.
To avoid some kind of administrative problem in the future, perhaps we should pass a motion in this Chamber, by unanimous consent, that might incorporate the notion that when bells begin to ring, if either the Whip of the Official Opposition or the government Whip approaches the Table and indicates that they intend to use the maximum amount of time, then the clock appear on our television screens.
I would like to hear from other members in the Chamber, independent members, or from the Whips' offices of the New Democratic Party or the Official Opposition. I think now is a good time to resolve that issue so members will have certitude about votes in the future. Nothing is more important for us than the maximum amount of certitude about when votes are required and in particular a non-confidence vote.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this is all very interesting. I too liked the clock that was available for members of Parliament on the television screen for those of us who are in our offices, at committee meetings or elsewhere on Parliament Hill.
I do think that perhaps this issue should be discussed at the House leaders' meeting. Essentially, what the Chief Government Whip is proposing sounds eminently reasonable. But the floor of the House of Commons is a rather unusual place to have a House leaders' meeting.
Probably more fundamental than anything raised by the Chief Government Whip is the fact that the supply convention of this House is such that before granting supply to the government, this House has a right to air its grievances. This is a supply day today, as is Monday. Surely, our time should be spent airing the grievances of the people before the Government of Canada before deciding whether or not we shall grant this government supply. That would probably be a better use of our time at this point than the issue we are discussing right now.

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I find it interesting that on an opposition day the Chief Government Whip has chosen to raise this particular motion. There has been ample opportunity all week to raise it privately with representatives of the other two parties.
I, for one, like the compromise that has been suggested. I would prefer if members of the Liberal party had not always caved in to work with the government to short circuit our delaying of the House, but so be it. That is their right.
I would suggest that we move on to Orders of the Day and that we leave matter this for the House leaders to work out.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I believe that this issue, according to our patterns of behaviour, is really a Whips' issue. It is the Whips who have the defined responsibility. There have been some consultations. I would like to seek unanimous consent of the House for the clock to appear when the bells begin today.
We have an important confidence vote on a Friday, a very unusual circumstance, and I would like you, Madam Speaker, to ask the House whether there is unanimous consent for the clock to appear on the television screen today when the bells begin to ring. I would give my assurance that I will not walk down the aisle until the maximum amount of time has elapsed.

May I suggest, Madam Speaker, that we move to Orders of the Day.

speakeroldname: Mr. Albert Cooper (Parliamentary Secretary to Government House Leader):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
I, too, rise on a point of order, Madam Speaker, that is somewhat in the same subject area, but which is a very different point. That is the question concerning what I believe has become a habit in the last while of members explaining their votes or rising after votes to make comments.
It is my understanding that once the House has divided, that ends the question. I have just taken the liberty of going through the last three months' of Hansard to look randomly at votes. Very often, people say things such as, and I quote from page 7436 of Hansard'.

Mr. Speaker, unfortunately I missed the vote. Had I been here, I would have voted nay.
At page 7659 of Hansard, there is another explanation:

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I was inadvertently delayed, but for the record I want to indicate that had I been here for the vote I certainly would have voted against government-
For that particular day, there is almost a page and a half of interventions recorded in Hansard making various explanations about the votes that happened on that day.
Here is another really interesting one. At page 8724 of Hansard, there is Division No. 195 which was eventually defeated. What I find interesting is that Miss Grey rose in her place and said:
Mr. Speaker, I would just like it to be on the record that I am in
the Chamber at present and am choosing to abstain on this motion.
Then it goes on with various comments from there. There are all sorts of comments. Mr. Benjamin said:
Mr. Speaker, I also rise on this point of order. There is no such
thing as an abstention in the House of Commons.
It continues on for a page and a half.
Point of Order
What is clearly happening is that our tradition of having the vote and that being the end of it is being eroded. Now, on a regular basis, we have members rising in the House to say: "Madam Speaker, I was late coming in. Had I been here I would have done this, I would have done that or I should have done this". It is prompting a whole round of points of order.
Our rules are very clear. If we look at at Citation 223 on page 75 of Beauchesne's fifth edition, we see that it states the following:
(1) A Member must be within the House and hear the question put in its entirety, in one of the official languages, or his-
-and one would "her"-
-vote cannot be recorded. It is not sufficient for him- -and I add "her"-
-to hear it while he is in a gallery or behind the curtains.
Beauchesne's is very clear. If a member wishes to vote on a item, he or she must be in their place in the House. To stand up later and say: "I'm sorry, I wasn't here," and then try to explain to their constituents that they would have done such and such, I believe is an abuse of the rules, an abuse of members' time, and an abuse of House time. It is something that is clearly unacceptable.
The book entitled Precis of Procedure is a helpful book. On page 53, under Recorded Divisions, it states:
Recorded divisions are conducted formally according to various
rules and practices. Standing Orders permit no further debate when
Members have been called in to a division, and specify that when the
Speaker is putting a question-
-and this is the important part-
- no Member may enter, leave or cross the House, or make any disturbance. Members must be in their seats to vote, and must remain seated until the result of the vote is announced. A Member may abstain from voting simply by remaining seated during a vote. Such abstention is not, however, recorded.
I just read an example a few moments ago of a member who abstained but then stood up and drew the attention of the House to the fact that she had abstained. It is that kind of thing that has been developing lately that I think is wrong. I think it needs to be corrected because the rules on voting are very clear-a member is to be in his or her seat to hear the motion put. They are to vote if

March 23, 1990
Point of Order
they choose. If they choose to abstain, then they are to remain seated.
What I think has been going on is something that needs to be arrested. I want to bring it to the attention of the Chair and ask that the Chair give it very serious consideration and bring back to this House the tradition and practices that we have followed in the past.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Madam Speaker, again all of this is very interesting. I have had an opportunity to discuss the issue with my colleague, the hon. member for Kingston and The Islands who is the opposition spokesman on the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. I am pleased to announce to my colleague across the way that we are willing to provide unanimous consent to refer this issue to that committee if that is the wish of the government.

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I note with interest that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Government House Leader did not indicate very clearly that it was government members as well as opposition and independent members in this House who have taken the opportunity to advise the House of their intentions had they been in their seats at the appropriate time.
I would like to concur again-and this is getting dangerous on a Friday morning-with my colleague from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell that a reference to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections be made to examine this matter. It would be more than appropriate. We would give our consent as well.

Madam Speaker, the sole point that I wanted to raise in response to the comments by the hon. member for Peace River is that there are occasions in the House where, by unanimous consent, a subsequent recorded vote is not taken in order to save everyone time and trouble in recording that vote. It is occasionally the case, and I have had the experience myself, where I wished to abstain on one of a series of votes but not on the others. In that event I suggest that the Chair ought to recognize that the procedure ought to accommodate the need for members not to delay the entire House by demanding full recorded votes but to
distinguish perhaps between motions on report stage where votes may want to differ.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, to respond to my friend for Ottawa South there are indeed certain circumstances where our rules provide for members to stand and declare a concern they may have with a particular vote, i.e. if they have a pecuniary interest, or if they were paired. Members have from time to time indicated: "Yes, Mr. Speaker, I was in my place. I would have voted but I was paired". It is part of the relationships that have developed over the years in the House.
When I rise on this point of order it is not simply to say it is the opposition members who are guilty of that. I think that we on this side have also done the same thing. That proves my case rather than refutes it because in fact what is happening is that we are keeping this practice going.
As it relates to the question of reference to a committee, I do not agree with that. I do not think we need to make a reference to the committee. Our rules are clear. Beauchesne's lays it out very nicely. We do not at this point need another reference to a committee. We simply need to go by the practices, traditions and longstanding habits we have in this House of Commons which I think on this particular subject have served us very well.
We do not need a royal commission. We do need a study. We just simply need to act on what we have to guide us in our present rules.

Mr. Speaker, I want to raise what I think is a very serious and important point of order arising from the discussion that took place, in particular the remarks of the member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan when he was making his presentation to the House. I do not want to prejudge this matter. Madam Speaker, you will have the opportunity to look at the official records of the House to determine exactly what was said.
My hearing indicated to me that what the member for Thunder Day-Atikokan said-and I think he was responding to the member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell in the exchange-went along these lines, Madam Speaker, and I want you to carefully note what I am saying. The member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan, as I heard his remarks, accused the member for Glengarry-

Prescott-Russell of not co-operating in the delay of the House. I think he said: "Cave in to the government", in not co-operating in the measures to delay the House.
If I read the rules of the House and authorities such as Erskine May, I see it is a very serious matter to delay improperly the process and proceedings in this House of Commons.
It is also very clear under our rules that the Speaker of this Chamber has the authority to remedy any attempts by members of this House to obstruct and delay the proceedings of the House.
I hope, Madam Speaker, that you would call the attention of the Chair to those remarks which evidence what we all know has been going on in this House of Commons day after day, week after week-an intentional delay of the processes and procedures of this House in order to obstruct government business.

You are saying that they are showing contempt for the rules, processes and procedures of this House. I am not making that charge myself. I am simply saying, examine the words spoken by the member for Thunder Bay-Ati-kokan, recorded in the official records of this House and determine whether that does not evidence an intention to improperly delay the processes and procedures of this House; and not only do they have this intention, as evidenced in these remarks, but they are even accusing other members of not co-operating in this improper, unfair action, an action that could never be said to be in the interest of Canada, and never could be said to be in the interest of parliamentary process or procedure.
We have rules in this House, rules that are fairly made, made with the consensus of all members of this House. If there is a deliberate attempt to defy and obstruct those rules by causing unnecessary delay, then I think the Chair should take some action.
In summary, what I am saying is examine the words, they are on the official record. I believe the Chair will find, by reason of the accusation to cave in to the government made by the member for Thunder Bay- Atikokan and not co-operate in delaying the work of this House, there is sufficient evidence upon which a conviction can be based.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my hon. colleague from Halifax has raised one of the most serious issues which has been on the table since the commencement of this particular Parliament.
When we come to this Chamber as new members, we get our first copy of Beauchesne's and have a chance to look at our purpose in being here. The words that stuck in my mind right from the beginning were that this was the highest court in the land. It should be a place of dignity, decorum, and process, process which is fair to all members.
In the final analysis, while the people on the street might think that the Prime Minister is my boss or that the hon. member for Windsor West is the boss of the Liberals or the Leader of the New Democratic Party is the boss of the NDP, that is not true. All of us are subject to the same conditions in being here. Our bosses are the people of our riding. They send us here expecting us to conduct ourselves in a manner that will lead to thoughtful decision making and to legislation that operates in the best interests of Canadians.
You have to ask yourself, Madam Speaker, whether or not that has been happening in the last year and a half as often as it should and as well as it should. This week we saw pictures on television of members of Parliament with

March 23, 1990
Point of Order
blankets and pillows because a committee had to meet for 31 straight hours, the equivalent of 20 sitting days of normal meetings, simply to listen to a filibuster. Canadians had an opportunity to watch that on television and they saw the childish behaviour.
Another example perhaps underlines in clear-cut House of Commons terms that we have a problem, and it is a problem that perhaps in the final analysis only the Chair can resolve. One day this week, we were debating a very simple motion in our Standing Orders, that the debate shall not be further adjourned. That is a motion which sits there so that the House, in a specific instance on a specific day with a specific piece of legislation, can break the tyranny of the minority. The majority shall, in the final analysis, rule when and if it is necessary.
In previous Parliaments and in the history of this country that was necessary from time to time but infrequently. If we look at the precedents in the British Parliament or Parliaments around the world, this occurs when necessary but infrequently. In my time in this Chamber I can remember a filibuster around the Constitution which went on for several days. I can remember the ringing of the bells which blocked the House for several days and led to some different rulings from the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Did you charge the Chair, too?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: I suggest the member across the way- and if I could say it once again for the House-go back to the television tape on the night that the Chair was charged. He will not see me charging the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Only your House leader did.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
There was an instinct to charge and it was very difficult to remain seated in the circumstances, but I want it clearly understood that anybody who stands in this Chamber from now on and says that I charged the Chair is lying to the House. Because this is about the fourth time I have said this, I suggest that they are lying to the House deliberately, because it did not happen and parliamentary immunity does not entitle members of this House to stand in this place and charge a member with behaviour without putting their own seats on the line. If you think I charged the Chair, charge me in here; do it formally. Let's go to committee, and if I am right and you are wrong, resign. That is what a charge is all about. At a
later time today I want to get back to that on a question of privilege. I have another one about a charge. I made a charge in this Chamber, and I think charges are very serious.
However let me deal with the point at issue before us now. In a democracy, the majority cannot be the captive of the tyranny of the minority, yet there must be a process that allows free and fair participation by minorities. It is a balancing act which is largely in the hands of the Speaker and the House, if necessary, in the final analysis.
During the division earlier this week when we were debating the motion that the House shall not further adjourn, members of the NDP were shouting "34". They were counting. What does 34 mean? It means that on 34 separate occasions in the life of this Parliament, which is a relatively short life span, this House has had to take time and money to overcome obstruction by a majority vote in this Chamber.
We met for two weeks in December 1988. We came back in April, 1989 and we have met on a regular timetable since, but we have not really had even one year of normal sittings. Normal sittings are about 175 days and, according to the NDP, we have had to use the time of this House, the $1 million a day that this House costs, on 34 occasions to overcome obstructionism.
That is childish. In the junior high schools or the elementary schools of this nation, in any fraternal organization, in any church group or anywhere else in society, that kind of obstructionism would not be tolerated.
Is this obstructionism on matters of great principle? Do you know what we were debating in this Chamber this week when we had to move that motion? Minor changes in crop insurance affecting the farmers of this country, and in particular western farmers. Members of the New Democratic Party by and large come from western Canada. They did not even vote against the legislation in the final analysis; they simply blocked. At $1 million a day they block, they block, they block.
This week they read in the rules of this House that they had to give 48 hours' notice for a vote today and they embargoed the Table from telling members of the

House. That is blockage. It was never intended. It was never contemplated.
The Speaker ruled that we were right.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: The Speaker has ruled that procedurally in some kind of legal way correct, but it is a brand new sense of obstruction of causing a vote. We will watch, Madam Speaker. There are 40-some members of that party who are supposed to be here to vote this afternoon, and how many will there be?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party

I am talking about the New Democratic Party being incorrect in asking and putting the Table under the gun, in using a notice provision in the rules and then asking the Table not to tell. That is being legally correct, but there is nothing in that initiative that speaks of any concern for the taxpayers of this country.
Madam Speaker, do you know how many dollars this vote this afternoon is going to cost? We have members flying in from thousands of miles away because it is a confidence vote. Canadians understand the cost of an airline ticket. They read the newspaper ads for the bargains on airline travel. They may live in Calgary and have relatives in Nova Scotia. They find the bargain $350 to $400 ticket, plan ahead and go.
But they embargoed that information, and our members are having to fly in to this city today for a vote this afternoon. They may have had to cancel engagements that other people were paying for. They are also having to travel without the bargain tickets, paying full fare because it came at the last minute. How many hundreds of thousands of dollars are the NDP costing the taxpayers of this nation today, when in fact this vote could have occurred on Monday? There will be another vote on Monday and we will contrast how many members of that party are here for the vote today and the vote on Monday.
If they were really interested in representing their constituents in this Chamber, the people who pay their salaries and send them to this place, wouldn't they like to have a vote on a day they could be here? I predict that
Point of Order
they will probably have twice as many people here on Monday as they have today in support of their own motion, and yet they will have caused $50,000, $75,000 or $100,000 worth of taxpayer's money to be spent on extra travel because they would not tell us on Wednesday night that they had given notice.
Members left and went to Vancouver, Yellowknife, Newfoundland, and Boston to do the work that the taxpayers are paying them to do. Today, they cannot do that work because they are on airplanes and the taxpayers are paying for it. Maybe some of them can leave in time to get back to their ridings to work on the weekend and maybe some of them cannot even make it so they are missing two days' work. That is a waste of taxpayer's money that they are causing through some of kind of childish view that this place should be obstructed, hour after hour, day after day, on things they do not even oppose.
This week this Chamber sat late on Wednesday night under the conditions of the motion that the debate should not be further adjourned to finish a crop insurance bill that they did not even have the guts to vote against. They rose in this House and took a lot of time this week, after 31 hours of obstruction in committee, lots of television pictures with pillows and blankets, and then into the House with another $1 million worth of obstruction today on that. They stood in this House and obstructed and obstructed and obstructed.
The toll of 34 occasions is not my number. I sat here and listened to the music. They are bragging that in less than one full year of sittings in this Parliament they have obstructed this Chamber on an absolute minimum of 34 days, which is an absolute minimum of $34 million.
We do not move the motion of time allocation or that the debate shall not be further adjourned on the day things commence. For each of those occasions which they count and said what we have had to do to overcome their obstruction, there is at least one day that precedes it and the doubling of 34 is 68. In reality in this Chamber alone, let alone committees, they have obstructed to the tune of a minimum of $68 million in less than one year.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my friend from Halifax raised the issue of obstruction in the Chamber. We have had a previous debate in another circumstance this week about the role of the Speaker in relationship to obstruction. The debate in a procedural sense is engaged. At what point does the Speaker act in the face of obstruction? At what point does the Speaker protect the democratic institution called the Parliament of Canada from the tyranny of the minority?
March 23, 1990

Surely any objective reader of parliamentary history, going back for decades and centuries, knows clearly that there is a role and a place for the Speaker of a Chamber to act, to seek the concurrence of the House that the actions are justified, that they are warranted in the individual case. He does that when the whole democratic process as expressed through its institutions is captive of a minority whose sole purpose, aim or objective is to be obstructive.
I suggest to you, Madam Speaker, that some other colleagues would like to give you a few examples of that obstruction. There is such a large menu that this debate could probably go on forever. The piece of evidence I bring to your attention is the behaviour of members of the New Democratic Party on Wednesday of this week during the vote that was caused by the acceptance of the motion that the House shall be no longer adjourned. They were using "34" and bragging that they had obstructed this Chamber, in less than one normal year of sittings, on 34 separate days. That is not evidence that comes to the Chair from members on this side of the House or from the Official Opposition. That is evidence which members of the NDP provided to the Chair themselves this week during the course of a vote.
The issue is: Shall it continue? Is the norm going to be that the House has to address itself to obstructionism 34 times every year? Remember, the House will not address itself to obstruction on the first occasion or the second; quite often it is the third or the fourth. Those 34 occasions represent an absolute minimum of 68 days of House sitting time and realistically probably about 102 times, which represents half the budget of this place. That is well over $100 million of taxpayers' money that is being spent on nothing constructive, nothing positive and nothing useful for the nation; simply on obstruction.
I suggest, Madam Speaker, that we have to think it through. Perhaps the Speaker would like to deal with the parties informally to try to resolve it in that fashion. It cannot be allowed to continue indefinitely. This place is too important. Democracy is too important. We must have a process which is fair and a process which ultimately acts in the best interests of the taxpayers of this country and of the voters of this country. That is the importance of this particular point of order.
Point of Order

Madam Speaker, I rise on the so-called point of order. I have two points to make.
First, I want to remind the hon. gentleman to remind himself of who rang the bells in this place for 15 days, and an agreement was reached on exactly the same proposal at the beginning of the 15 days in order to end the bell ringing, so he is in no position to talk.
Second, the hon. gentleman is asking the Chair to intervene in the proceedings of the House when there has been no violation of the rules. The Chair will intervene when members of the House conduct themselves in violation of the rules. That has not occurred, and whenever it has the Chair intervenes. For the hon. gentleman to ask the Chair to intervene when no rules have been violated shows a great deal of ignorance and lack of respect for this House.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I want to take a couple of moments to speak to the question of obstruction. I think it goes to the fundamental roots of Parliament. There are two elements to that debate. There is a question of whether or not the minority has the right to be heard and whether or not the majority has the right to govern. It has been a fundamental principle that in the end the government must have the right to govern.
One thing I find very significant is that closure was not used often by the previous government. Why was it not? The reason was very simple. It was because we as an opposition believed that at the end of the day the government had the right to govern. We never had to and never did behave in such a way that the government of the day would have had to use closure 34 times.
It is fundamental that Parliament has to be able to function. The government has to be able to govern. Equally, the opposition has to be able to debate. We have seen example after example in this House where time after time, through the filibustering obstructive tactics of the NDP, members of all parties including the opposition and the government have had to sit in their places and not be able to debate. After three or four days

hate groups and open demonstrations of anti-Semitism in the streets of Moscow.

Madam Speaker, the Prime Minister of Canada addressed the nation in the following terms:
Generations of Canadians have accomplished things they would never have dreamt were possible: in an untamed environment, they built a civilization; in their isolation, they found a love for this country; in their communities they developed the spiritual and family values that enrich our nation. It is these simple and strong values that made Canada. Today I want to ask all Canadians to look into their hearts and discover that magnificent country we have built together.
We are all privileged, francophones and anglophones, old and new Canadians, from Newfoundland to British Columbia, all without exception, to have made our homes in such a magnificent country. The problem we are facing today is not merely a constitutional deadlock or a debate among politicians. We, as heirs to one of the most beautiful countries in the world, are struck by the example of those who built in North America the home of tolerance and generosity. I urge all Canadians to close ranks and build together, with pride and determination, this beautiful, vast country we want to leave to our children.
March 23, 1990

Madam Speaker, since March 7, Mr. Bill Ripley of the Action for Social Change organization in Kingston, has been protesting Canada's complicity in Indonesian acts of genocide in East Timor by a hunger strike. The strike is now in its seventeenth day and will end only when the Canadian government meets his organization's demands.
Action for Social Change wants the Canadian government to condemn Indonesian crimes against humanity in East Timor and calls for that country's right of self-determination. Since 1975, over 200,000 lives have been lost through war and starvation in East Timor. As a member of the United Nations Human Rights Commission, Canada has failed to complain on behalf of the people in East Timor.
I call upon the government, today, to press the government of Indonesia to work toward an equitable resolution of this situation. The suffering of these people must be noted, condemned and ended immediately, and the Canadian government must show some leadership.

Madam Speaker, tomorrow marks the tenth anniversary of the murder of Archbishop Oscar Romero of El Salvador. Canadians will be marking the day with memorial services across the country.
The martyrdom of Archbishop Romero has become a symbol for all who walk the courageous path toward peace and justice in Central America.
Romero understood that true peace in Central America could only come from the people. He advocated liberation theology and the empowerment of those who were disenfranchised. Archbishop Romero died trying to realize the goal of justice for all.
Since the murder of Romero, there have been minimal attempts to investigate or punish those responsible. Instead, there has been a recurring pattern of death and repression of church and humanitarian workers. The recent brutal slaying of six Jesuits at the University of
Central America prompted an initial investigation, but it has stalled and those implicated are being promoted or sent abroad.
As we mark the anniversary of this tragic event, we are encouraged by news that the FMLN and the ARENA government have agreed to renew negotiations. In memory of Oscar Romero and for the sake of all Salvadorans, we hope and pray that these talks will lead to peace in El Salvador.

Mr. Speaker, experts from across the world gathered this week in Vancouver for Globe 90. Canada's policies came under the spotlight and rated poorly on almost every count. The head of the United Nations Environment Program, Dr. Mostafa Tolba, slammed Canadian forestry policy for contributing to the greenhouse effect by cutting down four trees for every one that we plant.
Forty per cent of the marine pollution in Canada comes from pulp mills and despite being the largest
industry in Canada and providing the largest source of balance of trade, there is no inventory. There is not even a plan for protecting old growth forests and some provinces like Alberta are planning to cut over one third of the entire province.
Three out of four Canadians consider our forests to be a national treasure held in trust. Three out of four think forest management is poor and that the industry is a threat. Nine out of ten believe spraying is a hazard according to the Environics poll released at Globe 90.
The federal government provides less than 10 cents out of every tax dollar raised from the forest sector back to that sector; the same level as the Liberals under Pierre Trudeau.
Globe 90 and the head of UNEP have set the record straight. There is not sustainable development going on in Canada's forests. We are cutting four times as many trees as we plant. Forest companies and government should stop lying about the facts. That is the message of Globe 90.

Mr. Speaker, it is interesting that the member raises that question. We had meetings with the Canadian Wheat Board a week or so ago. The Wheat Board indicated to us that while the export enhancement program has the effect of depressing prices, as do the subsidies that are paid by the European Community, which the hon. member knows are considerably higher than those being paid by the United States, this has not
March 23, 1990

affected Canadian market share. We are still maintaining our share and maintaining our traditional customers.
The hon. member asks what we are doing. We have certainly filed our notices through the appropriate diplomatic channels and I have spoken personally with Secretary Yeutter, reminding him of the commitment that has been made under the free trade agreement.
I should say as well that while we hear a lot about the amount of money that is being spent under the export enhancement program, in the range from $560 million to $900 million, in the period June 1989 to January 26, 1990 some $178 million Canadian was provided under the export enhancement program. So, I think it has to be put into perspective.
In the meantime, the Europeans are subsidizing exports of grain and oilseeds to the tune of $5 billion to $6 billion annually. What we have here is a situation of the United States responding to the actions of the European Community and Canada being caught in the cross-fire.

Mr. Speaker, the minister's defence of the U.S. is very obvious, but we are being forced out of traditional markets. Our major sales last year were not to the U.S.S.R., not to China, not to the EEC but to Iran, which usually was about twelfth or thirteenth on our list of sales.
Export enhancement was used six times in January to boost our sales to the U.S.S.R. So it is affecting our markets. If the Americans are giving more money it is going to escalate the trade war. That is going to affect the whole grain structure to the extent that it eliminates the psychological feeling that grain is the basis for the western Canadian economy.
When is the government going to assure the farmers that it is backing them by giving them enough money to seed the crop this year since seeding time is coming very quickly?

Over 18 million such returns came in last year and our observations of those returns showed that approximately the same amount of people last year used outside tax consultants and assistance as had in previous years.

Maybe the problem is one that was identified in the PC task force report on April 8, 1984. It states at page 5: "One of the problems in national revenue is that there has been a tradition of weak and junior ministers of national revenue", a tradition that continues today.
Another study done by the University of Montreal showed that the average taxpayer who requires outside help spends $349 a year for that help or a total of $5.5 billion in 1986 before tax reform. I assume it is much higher after tax reform.
In light of those facts, why has the Conservative government gone back on a promise it made in 1984 and 1985 to simplify the tax form and save the taxpayers of this country a great deal of money? Why has it not fulfilled that promise?

Madam Speaker, Wednesday, March 21, marked the second annual Rural Revitalization Day.
Rural Revitalization Day is the day proclaimed and set aside by Rural Dignity of Canada and observed by Canadians who understand the proud rural roots of this great country. It is a day to honour Canadian rural communities and to draw public attention to the extremely serious problems currently faced by too many rural communities.
As can be seen clearly, the purpose of this motion today is not to condemn the government. Rather, it calls for continued efforts on the part of government to develop policy and modify existing policy with the aim of strengthening the economic and social base on which communities can grow.
What is rural Canada? More than 90 per cent of Canada is rural. There are 9,000 small communities, cities, towns and villages, as well as several hundred thousand farmers, fishers and other rural dwellers in various occupations.
The industries of rural Canada are farming, fishing, forestry, mining, tourism, transportation and dozens of other locally suitable occupations which supply services to other rural Canadians.
Almost every raw product that cities demand and need come from rural communities. Be it cereals, oil, power, lumber, gravel or even drinking water, they all come from outside city limits. The people who produce, mine or just care for these products are residents of rural Canada.
Almost all of Canada's natural resources and a good part of our human resources are found in that vast area we call rural Canada. Despite having all these rich resources, rural Canadians face a bleak and unpromising future. Farming and fisheries particularly are going through a catastrophic economic time so severe that the future of thousands of Canadians and thousands of farm and fishing families are in immediate and at serious risk.
If urgent government action is not taken, these people will be forced out of business. They will follow their sisters and brothers, sons and daughters to the cities. Their rural communities will wither and die, which deaths will be to the detriment of not only rural Canada but all the rest of Canada as well.
Saskatchewan has been losing 20 residents per day throughout the winter. That is one every hour or so. That means that since the last federal election two towns the size of Humboldt which is my constituency have disappeared from Saskatchewan, or five towns the size of Rosthem, also in my constituency, have disappeared from rural Saskatchewan.
It has been obvious for some time that social, economic and technological changes are aspects of rural life that are resulting in major dislocation and stress in families and individuals in rural Canada. The main concern of farms on the prairies these days, and to a lesser extent across Canada, is the farm debt which is debilitating and causing a considerable amount of concern. Also, the amount of return the farmers are getting from crops and livestock that they raise is so little that they are unable to finance those debts and maintain a fair level of living.
In Saskatchewan alone, out of 61,000 or so farmers,
20,000	are in some kind of financial distress. They are either being foreclosed on or finding themselves in difficulty as far as continuing farming is concerned. All farmers in Saskatchewan, except those who are able to finance themselves, are having difficulty borrowing funds to plant this year's crop. This lack of operating funds is forcing more people off the farms. The impact of having to change one's vocation is much greater than someone who is just changing a job.
The farmer who loses his or her land is forced out of farming. The stress is much greater than would ordinarily be the case in losing a job. It means losing a way of life. It means losing a heritage which may have been built over many generations. In many cases the grandfathers or great-grandfathers homesteaded those farms. They are losing the land that their great-grandfather built, cleared and made into a farm. They are losing the farm. They feel that they are betraying that heritage, the trust of their ancestors, and their children who might follow them on that particular land.

Farmers' sons or daughters do not just decide to start fanning at the age of 18 years. They do not just suddenly say: "I am going to take up agriculture and become a farmer". Most people who go into farming have lived on the farm and grew into farming. It is part of their life from their first days after birth. Losing it is like losing that life.
Fishing families have had much the same heritage. Taking them out of the vocation has the same devastating impact as it does on farmers. The stress and loss of confidence to which this leads causes a considerable amount of dislocation and things happen which would not ordinarily happen in those structures.
In my home province we are seeing a tremendous increase in family break-ups in the rural areas. We are seeing a tremendous amount of illness among farmers and farmers' wives, and young farms in many cases. We are also seeing physical illness, psychological illness and nervous breakdowns. The suicide rate has substantially increased, to the point where some psychologists are suggesting that in rural areas more than 50 per cent of the suicides are caused by the economic disintegration of the family farm.
Alcoholism has increased considerably. As in much of the rest of Canada and the rest of society, in bad times women and children suffer the most. When farming, fishing and forestry can no longer provide the requirements of a good life for the family, women and children are hurt the most.
The motion I have put before the House at this time recognizes the crucial role played by women in rural communities. On the farm they are often required to cany three jobs. Not only do they play a substantial role in the operation of the farm; they also raise the family, take care of the house and make sure the meals are cooked. Today, a large percentage of farm women, nearing 50 per cent, work off the farm to bring in some needed cash so the farm can survive. The motion pays special attention to the role of women and the need for support of women in these circumstances.
The impact in rural areas is one of depopulation, not only in farming communities but in fishing communities and in a large part of the rest of rural Canada.
Most city folk consider living in rural Canada sort of idyllic, but it is only idyllic as long as the necessary
Supply
services to raise a family are in place. They will tell me how lucky I am to live on a farm where it is quiet and serene. It is, and I appreciate it. It is getting more and more difficult to raise a family in those circumstances because the services that are necessary to raise a family, such as education, health services and recreation, are becoming less and less available in rural communities. Rural hospitals, post offices, schools and other service centres are being shut down without any regard for the needs of the people who remain in those communities.
It is time to recognize the immense benefits we derive from these rural and their resources and return to rural Canadians a fair share of the benefits they supply to Canada.
When an industry in a particular area becomes less viable the families start to move out. This depopulation leads to removal of services because the community cannot afford to pay them, or as happened in many cases lately because the government is trying to save some money and is no longer willing to provide those services. When the service people move out they reduce the population further so that more services are jeopardized, which leads to further depopulation. It is like a snowball rolling downhill which picks up snow and becomes larger as it moves down the hill. Or, it is like dominoes set up in a row; when you knock down one eventually all of them fall. We all know the solution if you want to simplify it enough: it is economic stability.
In the case of farming the debt would have to be dealt with as well and first. Most farmers have learned to deal with the variables of raising a crop, fluctuating prices and intransigent weather. On a day to day basis the threat of losing the farm eats into the hope and eventually causes such tremendous stress that psychologically it is difficult for those people to continue. On the farms we must first deal with the debt and, second, we must deal with stable economic income.
Fishing communities are in much the same situation. They face the same kind of extinction in many cases. Again there is a need for the community to survive during a crisis. In the case of fisheries, it is necessary that the available fish provide income to communities and to develop the fisheries to the point where they can expect to continue in those areas. I could go on to talk about forestry and other industries relative to rural Canada

which are being affected these days in much the same
way.
In closing, I want to take a moment to pay special tribute to Rural Dignity of Canada. Rural Dignity is a network of Canadians working together to develop public awareness of the problems facing rural communities. Rural Dignity is more than that, however. It is a committed group of people who work to find realistic solutions to the problems faced by rural communities throughout Canada. Rural Dignity is to be commended for efforts to strengthen the economic and social base of rural Canada.
I want to quote two excerpts from press releases and news items which have come out of write-ups of the Rural Dignity:
Towns and villages are ecosystems as fragile as any marshland or northern shore. The social and economic well-being of our small communities, their relation to one another and with the entire country rests on a delicate web of interdependent threads: post offices, trains, local fish plants and grain elevators, family farms.
That is the kind of concern that Rural Dignity has been showing for what is happening to rural Canada.
It is my fervent hope that all members of this House, on both sides of the Chamber, will reflect on the difficulties experienced today by thousands of farming and fishing families, dwellers of rural Canada.
This motion was intended to be, and is, a very positive motion. It does not condemn the government. It does not look into the past to say anything about who should accept the blame. It talks only about sustaining rural Canada. It does not blame anyone. This motion points out the need of action if rural Canada is going to survive. It attempts to tell all of us how important and valuable rural Canada is, and how it is important, not only to those rural Canadians, but to the rest of the nation. This motion, as far as possible, is intended to be a vehicle. It is an attempt to draw attention to the way of life that is important to Canada and the basis for the heritage of many people in the country.
This motion points out the devastation of rural Canada does not have to happen and that we should make a commitment now to provide the economic, social and environmental atmosphere to have a sustainable rural Canada. Consequently, I hope that all members here today can find it in their hearts to say, yes, even if we cannot do it today or tomorrow, we will make a commitment to make sure that rural Canada can survive in the next few years. We need rural Canada as much or more than we need the strengthened economy of the cities.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak about a subject that is very near and dear to my heart. I want to associate myself with many of the comments that the hon. member outlined when talking about the amenities of rural life and the very special life-style that it provides to so many people, particularly those who are involved in farming, fishing, mining, forestry and the tourism industry.
His motion does zero in on a number of items such as stabilizing the family farm income and the debt situation. I would want to seize the opportunity to place on the record some of the initiatives that our government has taken in that regard.
The hon. member talked about the fishing communities and the fact that we all recognize that there are some difficulties in the fishing industry and in the Atlantic region particularly. We are addressing those problems, first, with a commitment of $130 million that was provided as an interim measure of support. As well, as the Prime Minister and the Minister of Fisheries have indicated in the House, we are working on a package which, hopefully, can be announced fairly soon to help resolve some of the difficulties that result when the stocks of fish are declined to the extent that it does affect the rural communities in a very devastating way.
He talked as well about transportation, the need to have an adequate transportation infrastructure, and to ensure that that transportation system is efficient, effective, and does provide the necessary links for commodities and people to travel. In the course of my experience as a cabinet minister, particularly as Minister of Transport, we embarked upon a program of regulatory reform which freed up the system enormously. I must say that I get a tremendous amount of satisfaction when I land in Halifax, for example, and I see all the commuter aircraft parked at the Halifax air terminal. They provide service to many of the smaller communities that never had service before.
March 23, 1990

The same applies in Edmonton and Calgary and perhaps even more so in Vancouver where the smaller communities are linking up with the major carriers, providing regular service and greater frequency of service. Maybe they are not flying jets, but what they are indeed flying are products built here in Canada, such as the de Havilland Dash-7 and Dash-8. That really demonstrates how one can integrate the policies of transportation with economic polity not only to improve the transportation system for all Canadians but indeed to create jobs in those very important industries.
Rural life is very special. I certainly associate myself with the words of the hon. member. There is a sense of hardiness and a sense of community. There is a sense of community discipline and a pioneering spirit that is evident in smaller communities. There is a sense of self-reliance. There is a sense of co-operation and support in smaller communities. One of the great gifts of a small community is that if you are ever in trouble as a citizen there, you are never alone. Your neighbours and friends are the first ones there to help you. As a result of that attitude, there has been a tradition developed in these communities. It is as alive today as it was when the rural areas were first settled. There is that clear gift of helping each other and co-operating. I am sure the hon. member would agree that it was in that spirit that many of the co-operative movements sprang up in western Canada, movements which are still in effect today.
I know that there are many problems in the rural communities. But even today what is most satisfying is to go to a community and see the citizens roll up their sleeves to build a community hall, a curling rink, an arena or a cultural facility. I am sure the hon. member, as I do, has opportunities of opening these facilities. With a certain amount of government assistance provided at both the federal and provincial levels, we provide that kind of additional stimulus to ensure that spirit of co-operation and reaching out to help each other is nurtured.
Clearly, from my perspective, rural life and agriculture are really synonymous. As agriculture changes, so does the environment within our rural communities. It is true that the agriculture industry, particularly in western Canada, has gone through turbulent times in the past few years. Many people overlook this but we had a drought situation that was worse than what was experi-
Supply
enced in the Dirty Thirties. The fact that farming and farmers have survived is a tribute to their resilience and a tribute to the fact that governments have in fact responded to this particular challenge.
We have trade wars resulting in low commodity prices. We have had other weather related disasters. In some areas, we have had excessive rain and flood situations. We have had grasshoppers. We have had the problem of increasing input costs. We have had the problem of changes in the market-place.
In Question Period earlier today, I outlined the fact that today the European Economic Community is no longer one of our major customers. It is one of our major competitors. As a matter of fact, it is the second largest exporter of grains and oilseeds in the world. That has an impact on us within our own agricultural industry and it also has an impact upon the rural communities relying upon it for their sustenance.
There have been changes in consumer demands. People are eating different things and placing priorities on different articles of produce. That has to be taken into consideration. Above all, there have been changes in technology.
All these elements have made it necessary for agriculture to adjust and to change and that has had an impact upon our rural communities as well. There is, particularly, the devastating reduction in incomes as a result of drought and other weather related disasters. Bear in mind that we had programs such as stabilization and crop insurance in place hopefully to respond to these. But, the experience of the past number of years demonstrates to us that these programs have not been adequate or sufficient. The result of this has had a major impact upon market receipts, particularly in western Canada.
I would like to read into the record the market receipts over a five-year period. These are market receipts in western Canada because that is what the hon. member was referring to primarily. In 1984, the market receipts were $6.5 billion; in 1987, the market receipts dropped to $4.6 billion, a drop of almost $1.9 billion in the marketplace; in 1988, they strengthened to $5.1 billion; in 1989, they strengthened more to $5.6 billion; and in 1990, the year about which everybody is very concerned, market receipts have gone down slightly but not nearly as

March 23, 1990
Supply
dramatically as they did between 1984 and 1987. At $5.3 billion, obviously there have been other factors that have been taken into consideration. What I am saying here is that with that decline in revenue from the market-place, clearly farmers would not have been able to survive without massive government support. I would like to put that into perspective.
In the period of 1981-84, the average realized net income in the agricultural community in Canada averaged $3.1 billion. In the period 1985-89, it averaged $4 billion, an increase of about 30 per cent. Direct assistance provided by the federal government in 1981-84 averaged about $600 million. Direct government assistance provided by the federal government in the period 1985-89 amounted to $2.5 billion on average. That is over a fourfold increase. It does not matter how you slice it, there has been massive government support.
In terms of federal support for all of agriculture, in the period 1981-84 it averaged at $2.3 billion and between 1985-89 it averaged $4.6 billion per year. That is a twofold increase. I think that is very important to keep in mind because we certainly have to give credit where credit is due.
What is more important, and I want to point this out, is that there has been a dramatic increase in support at the federal level over what the provinces have been providing. In terms of the total government support package, federal government support rose from 60 per cent in the early 1980s to over 75 per cent in the latter part of the decade. In the prairies, it has risen. For example, in the period 1981-84, Manitoba provided about 20 per cent of the assistance support and the federal government provided 80 per cent. In Saskatchewan, in that same period of 1981-84, the federal government provided about 85 per cent of the support and the province, 15 per cent. In Alberta, in that same period of 1981-84, the federal share was 45 per cent and the provincial share was 55 per cent.
To illustrate what I am saying, in the next five-year period, 1985-89, in Manitoba the federal share went up to 90 per cent and the provincial share dropped to 10 per cent. In Saskatchewan, in that same period, the federal share was at 87 per cent and the provincial share was at 13 per cent. And in Alberta, the federal share went up to about 65 per cent and the provincial share was at 35 per
cent. I think that clearly demonstrates the fact that the federal government has been there, as we have said we would be there, and we are there today.
A few other things have happened and I would like to put them on the record because it ties in to the first element of the hon. member's motion. That is the whole issue of providing income stability and dealing with the debt load. Let us just review the record.
I should say that federal assistance to the grains and oilseeds industry from 1981-84 amounted to $350 million annually. That is an average. From 1985-90, it amounted to $2.5 billion per year, a sevenfold increase to the grains and oilseeds sector.
Here are some of the other things that we did during the period of 1985-90. We placed a moratorium on foreclosures while addressing the serious financial difficulties being experienced by the farm community. That was from December 1984 to May 1987.
We brought in an $80 million, 4 per cent interest rate reduction program, reducing all Farm Credit Corporation loans at 16.75 per cent down to 12.75 per cent. It was at 16.75 per cent because, remember, we were coming out of that period of high interest that the Liberals were responsible for. It drove interest rates up to 24 per cent. That is what happened.
We introduced the shared FCC risk mortgage. We established the Farm Debt Review Board program. Some
9,000	applications have been handled by this program. There were 6,500 arrangements identified, meaning that 77 per cent of those using the board have reached an agreement. We committed $360 million to the Farm Debt Review Board to cover concessions, interest rate write-downs and write-downs on the value of the land. We have injected some $600 million into the Farm Credit Corporation, to cover loan losses. There is about $1.4 billion that needs to be written down.
As a result of the government assistance, a new band-aid, and considerable effort by the FCC, arrears have declined from almost 15,000 loans in fiscal year 1987 to 9,000 loans in February 1990. Of the 5,700 Farm Debt Review Board cases referred to by the FCC, 5,200 have been resolved. We established a $30 million Canadian rural transition program. We announced commodity-based loans. We passed a new farm improvement loan act. We brought in the two Special Canadian Grains Programs. We covered $300 million worth of losses in the
March 23, 1990

Canadian Wheat Board pool accounts. We covered $750 million in losses in the Western Grains Stabilization Act.
We contribute about $200 million annually for crop insurance and that is going to go up to $300 million. We paid out some $4 billion under the WGSA between 1985 and 1989, and I think that ratio was about $10 or $11 federal money for every $1 put in by the producer. We incurred a deficit in the federal crop insurance fund of some $500 million over the last four years as a result of payouts of $2.4 billion. We have improved the crop insurance program to include the multi-year disaster benefit relief program of which over $100 million has been paid out this year. We provided fuel price rebate relief of $200 million per year. We provided a total of $1.17 billion in emergency drought assistance between 1984 and 1988 and we brought in stabilization programs for the red meat industry, expending some $650 million to date. From 1984-85 to the present, we expended some $483 million for horticulture and eastern grain products through stabilization programs.
That in itself is quite a litany of achievements and I could go on. After 1984-85, we presented the five-year dairy program and provided $1.2 billion. We provided tobacco growers with $62 million, and grape growers with $128 million in transition assistance. What is encouraging is that both the grape and the wine industries are moving along very nicely, thank you very much, both in Ontario and in British Columbia. The fact of the matter is they recognize that adjustments had to be made. The federal government was there, and the provincial governments as well, to help in that adjustment process.
So, total government initiatives during the period 1984-90 have well exceeded some $22 billion. I could go on and talk about the improvements in the crop insurance program and the plant breeders' rights.
Today, I am announcing that the farmers living in the designated areas of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta are eligible for a one-year tax deferral on income derived from the drought-induced sale of breeding livestock in 1989. This is something that has been done before with regard to the serious drought problems in that particular region. There are other areas and we will be writing to the Minister of Agriculture for the province of Ontario which has some pockets of drought. Wherever there are pockets of drought based on forage yields of less of 50 per cent of the normal yield, this will trigger
Supply
that same initiative. But that again outlines the sensitivity that we show toward agriculture and how we put our money where our mouth is.
I said as well that there are changes in the marketplace. The European Economic Community is engaged in a massive subsidy program. It is enormous. As I said earlier, in the case of Canada we have a situation where it has switched from being a net importer of about 12 million tonnes of grain per year to being the world's second largest exporter of grains and oilseeds, roughly 25 million to 26 million tonnes projected for this year. It got there by huge subsidies.
I noted the OECD has estimated that total support for agriculture in OECD countries was over $250 billion U.S. in 1989. Of that, some $100 billion U.S. was provided for by the European Economic Community; $67 billion U.S. by the United States; and $60 billion by Japan. The bulk of it is being provided by those countries. We have talked about the levels of export subsidy support through the EEP. It is roughly in the range of $17 per tonne at the present time and the European Economic Community is at $80 per tonne.
Let us just look at what they are spending in terms of their export programs, intervention costs and production refunds. In 1986-and this is in Canadian dollars-the European Economic Community spent $4.5 billion in direct assistance which is geared essentially toward getting its market share. In 1987, it was $6.3 billion; in 1988, it was $6.4 billion; and, in 1989, it was $5.2 billion. Those are enormous amounts of money.
The United States, in terms of the export enhancement program, in 1986-87 spent $842 million; in 1987-88, $1,446 billion; in 1988-89, $545 million; and from June 1989 to January 26, 1990, $178 million U.S. One can see there why the Americans are responding to the Europeans because of the huge subsidies that are engaged in. That is a fact of life. We have to recognize that.
We have to find new customers for the grain that we marketed to the European Economic Community and the displacements which have resulted from their very generous export program. That is why we are committed through the MTN to the progressive reduction in tradedistorting subsidies. We are committed to achieving greater market access and to reducing the level of export subsidies. We are committed to reducing the level of internal support and to developing a more harmonized application of the rules as they apply to health and sanitary measures.
