The bottom line is that we want a rule book that applies equally to all. We want a rule book with no waivers and no variable import levies. We want a clear set of rules and that is why we are attempting to change Article 11 and bring it up to date to where it should be.
Changes in technology have also contributed very much to the impact upon rural life. Twenty years ago in western Canada, we had 5,000 elevators in operation. Today we have a little over 1,000. We have 1,600 to be exact.
The number of delivery points has gone down. In 1969 and 1970, we had roughly 1,800 delivery points. We are down to 1,000. Those changes have taken place. Those changes have impact upon rural communities. It is the changes in technology, in consumer attitudes, and in world trading patterns, and it is the impact that all of these things have upon the rural life-style and rural living. This government recognizes that. This government has responded to it in the past. This government will respond to that challenge with the farmers in the future.

Madam Speaker, I would like to thank the minister for participating in this very important debate and for giving us an opportunity to hear the contribution the federal government has made to farm life, particularly in western Canada. I would like to use a little broader approach than the one he has used to outline why the Canadian western economy is in such great trouble.
He took pain to point out that the contribution of the government of Manitoba-and far be it from me to fight for the government of Manitoba these days-has dropped down to 10 per cent, while the federal government's contribution has increased to 90 per cent.
In his answer, could the minister put that into the context of the cancellation of ERDA agreements, the decline in the amount of moneys available to the Western Development Fund, and the fact that, as the federal government has pulled out of other funding mechanisms, it has been necessary for the provincial
governments across western Canada, in fact, to protect their budgets from declining revenues and declining transfer payments.
Although I am not inclined to share many of the priorities of the provincial government in Manitoba, I think it is only fair for the record to indicate that it has had an increasingly difficult time for them, because the federal government has decided to change their funding strategy.
Second, would the minister perhaps address a question that the premier of Saskatchewan considers to be paramount in saving rural life in western Canada. That is approaching banks for relief on questions of interest rates? Could he indicate the extent to which the government is willing to get involved in seeing that the banks do everything they can to alleviate the pressures of western Canadian farmers?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there are about four questions there. I hope I can cover them all. They are very important questions and I appreciate them very much.
On the issue of the ERDAs, we have not cancelled ERDAs. ERDAs will be negotiated. They may have a somewhat different criteria, but the fact of the matter is that the hon. member talked about reducing regional development spending in western Canada and I would not want to leave the House with the impression that he has just suggested.
Quite frankly, compared to the period between 1980 and 1984, as compared to the current five-year period, western Canada's share of the national regional development funding pie has risen from 21 per cent to 32 per cent. I ask him to check that record. It is in the budget papers of April. I forget the page number, but I can give it to him if he would be interested.
The amount of money that has been provided for western Canada in the regional development fund has increased from a level of $500 million in the period 1980-84, when there was literally nothing going out to
March 23, 1990

the four western provinces. The fund for the current five-year period is $1.8 billion.
Are all those agreements signed?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, they are not all signed. That is wrong.
Then there is the western diversification initiative which the Liberals try to take issue with. I can say that some $715 million has been expended, covering 1,500 and some-odd different projects.
Expended or allocated?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Allocated. Talk to the people who get the consideration of the western diversification. The proof of the pudding lies right there. They are jealous because they did not do anything. They had a $4 billion vanishing fund that never saw the light of day. They spent $60 million out of it. It never occurred. The fact of the matter is that this is a very, very important initiative.
Right in his own area, and this again speaks to diversification and to the free trade agreement, Versatile Manufacturing was a basket case. The government worked out a recovery package with Ford-New Holland. At that time there were 300 people employed by Versatile. Today, there are over 1,100 employed by Versatile, thanks to free trade. If you heard what they are saying now about the GST, you would know that the combination of the GST and the free trade agreement will tilt more of the manufacturing into Winnipeg. That is the kind of regional development and the kind of broadening of the scope of the economic fortunes of western Canada at which we need to be working. That is what we are doing.
With regard to the question of the banks, I can tell the hon. member that I did attend a meeting with the premier to talk to representatives of the banks about the farm debt and the farm credit situation. It was a very good and a very constructive meeting. I think there are some things that can and will be done.
For our part, as it relates to the Farm Credit Corporation, we are looking at a number of options that we might be able to engage in with respect to extension of leases and with respect to modifying the farm debt review board process. This would provide greater latitude and greater
Supply
flexibility to farmers who are really trying to maintain a good credit rating and who have some obvious chance of success and viability. We are going to be adjusting that so that they can be accommodated in a more compassionate and beneficial fashion.
I appreciate the hon. member's question. I can assure him that we are looking at these things.
I should also say that the banks are only one component. They charge interest for the services they provide. We know interest rates are somewhat high. That is an input cost component. We also have to recognize that there are other cost components such as fuel, fertilizer and chemicals. We are also looking in those areas to see what we can do to bring down the prices.
There, again, the GST will bring down the cost of inputs by $240 million to $250 million across the country.
Don't push your luck, you were doing fine.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He should not laugh at that, because $250 million to fanners is a lot of money.

Madam Speaker, I wish to thank the minister for attending this important debate today. His concern for rural Canada is certainly noted by this side of the House.
He cited a lot of statistics and figures about the effort the government has made over the last couple of years concerning its support for agriculture and the rural economy. The people on the farms and in the small communities are looking for only one statistic-a statistic that shows they have a healthy economy in agriculture and in rural communities.
The minister is aware, since he alluded to it in his speech, that the health of the agricultural economy has a significant impact on the health of our rural community. If there is no money in agriculture, there is certainly no money in the rural community. If there is no money in agriculture, there are fewer farmers on the land. That means there are fewer people in the small town churches, in the school system, and fewer people who support the curling rinks and the community arenas. Obviously, there are fewer people who support the rural businesses that are the mainstay of keeping other people inside that small community.

March 23, 1990
Supply
If we have a strong rural community, a quality of life that is acceptable to the seniors and the young people in those smaller communities, then we need a strong commitment to increasing the value of agriculture.
In light of all of that, my question to the minister relates to the premier of the province of Saskatchewan, who earlier this week in a throne speech suggested that he had received a specific commitment from the federal Minister of Agriculture about the agricultural financial crisis. The premier of Saskatchewan, the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool and members of Parliament in this House from Saskatchewan have asked for a $500 million payment at the very least to help secure the health of the farm economy this year.
I am wondering what commitment the Minister of Agriculture made to the province of Saskatchewan which the premier of Saskatchewan spelled out. When will he deliver on that commitment?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to repeat again that the commitment of this government as provided in terms of extending money and resources to the farmers of Canada is unprecedented in the history of this country. There is no question about that.
There are still problems. That suggests that money alone will not solve all the problems. I am glad the hon. member agrees with that because there are certain things that happen beyond our control such as changes in market trends, such as the actions of other countries and their various priorities. There are changes with regard to consumer attitudes and tastes, changes with respect to greater emphasis on environmental matters and in particular changes with respect to technology.
The hon. member would agree with me that change in agriculture is a constant. It has always been with us and our ability to adapt to change is perhaps one of the reasons why we have been successful over the years.
I repeat again to the hon. member, recognizing that the period we have gone through in Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba from a precipitation and heat point of view-in other words, summed up as a drought-is far worse than it was in the dirty thirties. We all know what the dirty thirties did to that region of the country. We have gone through some difficult times, but
we have been able to survive, thanks to the resilience and ingenuity of the farmers and thanks to the support of both the federal and provincial levels of government. I do not think you can deny that.
I also say that the changes that have occurred in the rural community are in large part technological change. We are producing more with fewer farmers. We are producing more grain and we have fewer elevators. We are producing more grain and we have fewer delivery points. As I said, 20 years ago there were 5,000 elevators in western Canada. Today, there are roughly 1,500 to 1,600.
That's nothing.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The hon. member says that is nothing. I think it is something. Twenty years ago we had 1,800 delivery points. Today, we have just a little over
1,000.	Is he telling me that that does not have an impact upon rural life? You bet it does. You can't blame that on the Tories. You blame that on the ingenuity of the grain handling companies, the farmer-owned co-operatives because they know that they have to be competitive to survive.

Madam Speaker, I am certainly pleased to have the opportunity today to stand and speak for a few moments on the motion before the House which in part is calling upon the government to provide for a vital economic, social and environmentally sustainable future for rural Canada.
As has been discussed by previous speakers this afternoon, rural Canada is certainly a very important sector of our society. I think that we need to do more to explain to Canadians the importance of rural Canada in the society in which we live. It is a society that is changing for many reasons. I will touch on those reasons.
I would like to point this out to members of the House today and ask them to reflect on it for a moment. There are four creators of wealth in the world. One is forestry. One is fishing. One is mining. One is farming. There is nothing on the face of the earth that we use or see or need that does not come from one of those sectors. All of those are part of rural Canada. All of those make up
March 23, 1990

rural Canada. Some of them are a more populated sector of the rural area than others.
I also want to state that I have always and will always firmly believe that as goes agriculture, so goes the economy of any country. If we look around the world it does not matter how a country is trying to survive, if it does not have a strong, viable, economically strengthened agricultural industry, then the economy and the future of that country is certainly in question. I can give examples of that but I think as we stop and think about it they will come to the minds of all of us.
I said a few minutes ago that the rural community is changing. We all know that we are losing small towns in the prairies for different reasons. The industry is changing. We all know that in the more heavily populated parts of the country, urbanites are moving into rural areas in order to live the way of life that is there. As this takes place, I hope the government keeps in mind that we must still maintain what rural Canada is all about. In order to do that we must maintain the management tools. We must maintain and assist the abilities of the people in those communities-the farm people, the primary producers and the processors-in order to keep that economy going.
We also must keep in mind that we have a debt not only to ourselves but to our children, our grandchildren and those who will come afterwards. That debt is to rural stewardship, to the stewardship of the resources that we have. We spent a lot of time about 18 or 24 months ago on one of the greatest debates that this country ever had. I refer to the free trade debate. We spent a lot of time talking about oil and gas and water. We also spent time talking about agriculture. But I do not think we took the right tack. I do not think we recognized the importance of agriculture to this country.
We are all concerned about food safety and food quality. I call upon the government to recognize to a greater extent than it is at the present time that, yes, there may be a few added costs to producing food in Canada, but I think that Canadians are prepared to pay that cost, if necessary, if it is explained to them. We have the safest food in the world right now. I believe that if it is explained to Canadians, they do not want to get things cheaper in the short run and then realize that it may cost in the long run. They are prepared to pay in order to
Supply
produce that food at home so that we can have it produced under our own guidelines and under our own regulations so that we can continue to have that safe food supply.
Another aspect I want to touch upon is one that is in the motion today. The motion states in part:
5) provide a full range of services, including shelters, child care services and skills training to support the crucial role played by women in all rural communities.
A few years ago I served as a member of the Ontario Thsk Force on Health and Safety in Agriculture which went across the province of Ontario for a great number of hearings. It was probably brought out to me at that time more than ever the importance of women in agriculture and the role they play. We know that there are fewer and fewer farmers in Canada. We also know that a higher percentage of those farms are spearheaded by women. A higher percentage are owned, operated and controlled by women.
We also know that the role that ladies play in the operation of those farms is very, very crucial. Because of the economic times, on many farms in Canada farm women may very well have an off-farm job. As well as having the off-farm job, they have the household to maintain, the family to look after, and in many cases they also play a major role in the management and bookkeeping of that farm.
I can name many farms where, when it is payroll day or bookkeeping day, the farm women may very well be up at 4.30 or 5 in the morning in order to get the payroll ready for the staff if there is a number of them, or they work late at night in order to do it. We have to recognize that.
I call upon the government not to withdraw from any more programs. There have been a lot of programs withdrawn in the last two or three years by this government. The Nielsen report of a number of years ago pointed out several things in the agricultural field that should be addressed. I am certainly disheartened by the way the government has addressed the changes that have been made to the farm improvement loans which now makes them virtually non-existent. The fuel tax rebate has been taken away for the most part. The assistance programs for fruit and vegetables storage construction, which the federal government shared in, has expired.

March 23, 1990
Supply
The At and East program for assistance in freight rates for grains has been taken away.
As we have been discussing lately, there is disappointment in much of the farm community concerning the contribution that the federal government is going to be making to the crop insurance program to the extent of 25 per cent rather than to the 33 and one-third per cent as was requested.
I would like to touch for a few moments again on the role of the government in our request for it to pay attention, give assistance and provide the management tools to the whole rural community. As I say, the rural community is changing. The percentage of family farms or farm families that are there now compared to 10,15 or 20 years ago is different. The urbanites are moving into the country. The agricultural people are realizing that they have to change some of the ways in which they do some things. They need support for that. They need the assistance of governments in order to explain their way of life, explain to urban people what they are and that they have come into a new community. There may be noises, sounds and odours that they are not used to, but they need to be there.
Madam Speaker, I thank the House for the opportunity this afternoon to make a few comments on this motion. Again, I plead with the government to recognize these requirements of the rural community and not do anything more to take away from the rural community.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: There are five minutes of questions and comments. The hon. member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake.

Madam Speaker, I have a question for the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings.
Rural Dignity is a very important player in the whole picture of the rural crisis that is occurring right now. I am just wondering if the hon. member is aware of the activities of Rural Dignity in his riding and throughout other parts of the rural community. In particular, is he aware of the work that it is doing on behalf of rural residents who are fighting to maintain their post offices in rural communities right across the country.

Madam Speaker, in response to the hon. member, I will have to say that, to my knowledge, in my area of Ontario there is not an active Rural Dignity group. However, I am somewhat familiar with the work that it is doing and attempting to do, which is excellent work. But in my particular riding there is not such a group.

Madam Speaker, I would just like to pose the second part of my question again which concerns rural post offices. I am wondering if the member could tell me what is happening in his area with rural post offices, the closure of post offices, and what the rural residents in communities in his area might be doing about it.

Madam Speaker, we have had one or two rural post offices in our riding "consolidated", which was the word that was used. I do not think my rural area is any different from any other, in that the people are not at all pleased with what is taking place. I am pleased to say, in the last few years they have had some success in keeping some post offices open, when there were attempts to have them closed.
Quite honestly, within four weeks of being elected to the House, I was approached by Canada Post, which informed me that the post office in my own village was being closed. However, in working with Canada Post, we were successful in getting it to move it to another facility in the very same village.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity today to speak to a motion that calls upon the Conservative Government, in the week of the second annual Rural Revitalization Day, to take steps to provide for a vital economic and social future for rural Canada.
Madam Speaker, we must not forget that since the Conservatives came to power, this government made savage cuts in VIA Rail and caved in to GATT decisions when it should have protected Canadian farmers, especially Canada's dairy producers. Farmers in general are suffering as a result of the negligence of the government across the way, and when we look at our rural communities, a number of institutions such as post offices are disappearing.
March 23, 1990

In 1986, there were 5,221 rural post offices in Canada. Today, 400 of these post offices have disappeared, and according to the Canada Post corporate plan, they will all be gone ten years from now.

Madam Speaker, 10,000 people work in rural post offices in Canada, and 83 per cent of them are women. Once this project of shutting down rural post offices is complete, the government will have been responsible for the largest firing of women in the history of Canada-8,300 of them will have lost their jobs. That is the sad reality.
Last night, I attended a meeting in my constituency in the small village of Dalkeith. Dalkeith is a community in Glengarry county and, Madam Speaker, as you probably guessed from the name, it is a very Scottish name, indeed. In that village, Canada Post is now proposing to shut down the post office and replace it with a franchise.
Canada Post has what it calls a natural opportunity. It defines a "natural opportunity" as being that occasion in which a postmaster or postmistress resigns or dies. Therefore Canada Post then has the privilege of shutting down rural post offices.
Canada Post cheats every now and then. What it did in this case is it went to see the postmistress and offered her early retirement. In other words, the person was not even scheduled to retire. The person was not scheduled to have a "natural opportunity". When Canada Post does not have a natural opportunity, it simply creates one.
What did it do? It asked the postmistress to take an early retirement for a certain undisclosed sum of money. I am not blaming the postmistress. After all, if one has worked for a long time and one is given a financial opportunity to retire early, perhaps she is correct in taking that opportunity.
However, Canada Post did this without attempting to secure alternative space for the post office, or even alternative space for its privatized so-called retail postal outlet. Now we have a situation whereby we are losing the service in that village. We do not know whether anything at all will replace it.
There has been a post office in Dalkeith for 123 years. It serves 81 residences in the village and 283 residences
Supply
on rural routes for a grand total of 364. Assuming that there are three people per household, it means that this post office serves 1,000 people.
Last night at the public meeting 289 people signed a petition that was presented to me. That was 289 people who signed a petition right in that room. I know it was not signed in advance because I brought the form with me. They all signed the petition in that room. In other words, one-third of the whole population-man, woman and child in that community-was in the recreation centre last night in order to voice their concern about that rural institution we call the post office.
People do not drive for miles or take whole evenings of their time-one-third of the population does not mobilize itself-for no reason. It does so because it feels in its heart that retaining that post office is something important to the rural way of life.
I say to the minister responsible for the post office, who interestingly enough is the same minister responsible for building strip joints, that the people of Canada want to keep our postal institutions in this country. That has never been demonstrated any better than by what the people of Dalkeith did last night. I hope that the minister responsible for the post office listens to what the people of that community say.

Madam Speaker, in the last Budget brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), we saw that the consumer watchdog for Canada Post had disappeared.
The Postal Services Review Committee was eliminated by the Minister of Finance in the Budget speech. Interestingly, the minister responsible for Canada Post said in 1988 that:
- considering that Canada Post had become a viable operation and that its revenues came from postal service users, customers therefore had a say in a national and local issues.
This means that in 1988, the government's position was that consumers had the right to be heard to be protected if Canada Post made decisions that went against their interests.
We now see a situation where the Minister of Finance has eliminated this consumer spokesperson, this watchdog, as I said earlier. We could say the watchdog was muzzled by the Minister of Finance when he slashed the

Supply
Budget, a Budget that would otherwise have provided funding for the Postal Services Review Board.
So we have the following situation: Canada Post has a monopoly on postal services, a monopoly it needs, I must admit. It has a monopoly, and of course the Gouvem-ment is taking a hands-off position on Canada Post, ostensibly because it is a Corwn corporation and the government has no right to intervene. So we have a regulated monopoly that is accountable to no one. Perhaps we should say we have a deregulated monopoly, because there seem to be no regulations to prevent Canada Post from doing what it did, for instance, in the case of the Dalkeith Post Office or in other cases.
My point is, Madam Speaker, that in order to maintain the quality of life in rural areas, the government must reinstate this Postal Services Review Committee or Board.

Canada Post spends $17 million annually on advertising to tell us that it delivers the mail. Most of us, I would suspect, already knew that Canada Post delivered the mail. Most of my constituents know that already. Perhaps there are occasions on which it does not deliver the mail and it tries to tell us that it does, using these advertising methods.
However, the Postal Services Review Committee which was there to watch over Canada Post on behalf of consumers was eliminated because it cost the taxpayers of Canada $3.6 million to operate. If the government across the way really cared about the people of rural Canada or about the people of Dalkeith or of any other similar small community which sees itself in a dispute with Canada Post of the type that I previously described, then why did it not cancel the useless $17 million advertizing budget of Canada Post instead of cancelling the $3.6 million to keep the post office watch dog that was there for consumers?
I am pleased to have had this opportunity to speak on this debate today and to offer my support to my constituents living in rural areas, in the hope that the Government of Canada will finally recognize that rural Canadians deserve better than what they have received since 1984.

Madam Speaker, the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell and I have shared some opportunities to talk about the post office in the last six months, having sat on the Standing Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Government Operations. We are very much aware of the devastation caused to rural communities when a post office pulls out.
I want to ask the member who has just spoken so well about the need for government co-operation in maintaining post offices in rural Canada if he is aware of Rural Dignity's comments about post offices, that the post office is the heart of a community. Can he tell us whether he believes that the Government of Canada has a responsibility to maintain a federal presence and a post office in those rural communities?

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am grateful to my colleague for his pertinent question.
Rural Dignity has done great work in being an advocate for rural Canadians and for speaking to the importance of retaining the rural post office. As my colleague from The Battlefords-Meadowlake will know, in many rural communities the only federal government presence there is Canada Post. The only time you see a flag of our country, the kind which is right beside Madam Speaker's chair, is on the post office. The only place in many communities where you see the word "Canada" is on the post office. Now we are shutting down the rural post office, eliminating that federal presence and eliminating that important community point of rendezvous. To make matters even worse, Canada Post has now developed a new corporate logo wherein it calls itself "Mail-Poste". It has removed the word "Canada" from Canada Post.
At this juncture in which it is so important for us to use all instruments of national unity that we can muster, I feel it is absolutely unacceptable for Canada Post to be behaving in that manner.

Madam Speaker, it is indeed a privilege to speak today in support of this motion from my colleague. At the outset I would like to focus my comments on the preamble of his motion because March 21 was the one hundredth anniversary of the birth of Agnes MacPhail, the first woman
March 23, 1990

elected to this House and an untiring champion of the rights of rural Canadians.
To begin my remarks I would like to quote from Hansard of February 28, 1928. Although that was 1928, it says a lot about what is occurring here now in 1990. During the debate on the budget of that year Agnes MacPhail stated:
We have, for a young and rich country, a depleted and impoverished agricultural industry. In this young country agriculture has not held its own people, nor its power of place and influence. I regret it, but it is true.
It is still true. Many of the things that Agnes MacPhail struggled for in her years in Parliament we are still struggling for now. Agnes MacPhail was in this place for almost 20 years from 1921 to 1940 and then continued in the Ontario legislature.
To win her first nomination in 1921, she had to defeat 10 men and then overcome the shock in the community that a woman had won. She then won the first of five federal elections with a campaign that cost $600, all in $1 contributions. There were no special favours from Agnes. At 31 she entered a House that was hardly ready for her. She was patronized by the Mackenzie King government which offered her a suite of offices when other MPs had only one room. Agnes took one room. It was then room 605 which became Agnes' office for her career, and it is now redesignated as room 629-C. This week my leader unveiled a plaque to be placed on the door of that room to commemorate Agnes' time there.
Agnes also met outright hostility in this House but learned to deal with it. To the heckler who taunted: "Doesn't the hon. member wish she were a man?" she replied: "No. Doesn't the hon. member wish he were?"
These quotes are very in keeping with some of the debate that goes on in this Chamber even now, Madam Speaker, and as you are well aware, women do have an uphill struggle even now in this Chamber.
My remarks on this motion speak to the legacy that Agnes MacPhail has left for us as women to carry on. In the most recent budget, there have been radical cuts to women's programs. I was the volunteer chair of a women's centre in my community when the parliamentary committee travelled to Vancouver to talk about women's programs a number of years ago.
Supply
At that time the women's centres from all the rural communities came to Vancouver to plead their case as to why women's programs should not be cut, particularly for the rural areas. In this last budget they have been cut and the devastation that will wreak in rural communities is enormous. These women's programs are essential, especially in the north and in the rural areas. They are often the only resource for women who are battered by their husbands and are a release or safety net for women to go to. Yet, in the latest budget, the federal government has seen fit to cut them.
Another issue that Agnes MacPhail championed during her time here in the House was the commitment to social programs, particularly a commitment to child care. As a champion of rural issues, she knew the role that women played in their rural communities and the importance of child care in supporting that task.
Women had a very hard choice then. They either had to leave their children to go to work, or they had to take their children with them to go to work. Even now in Canada, in 1990, such is the case particularly for rural women. There is no national child care scheme. It was promised in 1984 and in 1988 it was promised, and here once again we have no commitment to a national child care scheme. This hurts rural women particularly. Their options are limited. Even in urban areas the people who are paying the price are the children of Canada. Agnes MacPhail knew that.
The comments of many members in this House speak of the destruction of rural Canada. This government is overseeing that destruction. Our party caucus has met with the mayors of the Canso communities, the rural fishing communities of Atlantic Canada, and the same sort of thing is happening on the west coast from where I come. This destruction of those rural communities and the fishing villages is because there is no commitment to understanding that communities want to control their own destiny and want to keep the jobs in their own communities. The government should be giving support in its programs for that kind of initiative.
There has also been much talk about the destruction of rural Canada through Canada Post regulations and lack of commitment. I know in part of my riding on the Gulf Islands the post office had been a community resource, and now that that has been taken away. This is something that is happening increasingly in Canada with this whole centralization of jobs and the increasing

March 23, 1990
Supply
dependency on the market as the determining factor. This is something that is very negative and is well addressed within the motion.
This government should be supporting programs to provide a full range of education, health and other social policies for young families to stay in their communities. We in this House know the kind of social problems that result from the urbanization of the population with people having no resource but to move into the cities, the abandonment of those small towns and the consequent destruction of the social life.
Agnes MacPhail in her time in this House was a champion of rural Canada because she was from rural Canada but also because she had that wonderful sense of community and of knowing that if we do not feel connected to where we come from then we have lost a great deal.
There are a number of other things that we can talk about on the anniversary of Agnes MacPhail's birth, 100 years tomorrow. She was also a champion of prison reform being a founding member of the Elizabeth Fry Society, and as a consequence she was the first woman to go into the Kingston Penitentiary. In another quote from that time she said she was told there were no ladies allowed in Kingston Penitentiary. She assured the people that she was no lady, she as a member of the Parliament. That is something that we as members of Parliament who are women have to realize too. Sometimes you have to become a member of Parliament to make sure that the dignity of women is assured, but you are a member of Parliament first and a woman second. I hope that that dynamic changes as more and more women become members of Parliament.
Agnes MacPhail was a champion, realizing that as the first woman member of Parliament she became an automatic voice for the women of Canada. The women members in this House should remember that they are the voice for the women of Canada; they provide a role model for the women of Canada.
Agnes MacPhail also worked for prison reform and equal pay for work of equal value. That is something that she championed, along with her colleague, Andrew Brewin. I have the privilege of having as my neighbouring constituency member of Parliament the son of Andrew Brewin. It is a nice little coincidence that the member for Victoria is now the critic for our party for the Solicitor General and is also still working on prison reform in the Kingston Penitentiary. The history of parliamentary action in our party is something of which we are very proud.
What we in British Columbia are facing with the destruction of rural communities coincides with Agnes MacPhail's concern for women in fishing communities and women in rural Canada. With the latest devastation brought about by the trade deal and the destruction of jobs which is occurring in the fishing communities in British Columbia, Agnes MacPhail would be turning in her grave, because women's jobs, usually immigrant women's jobs, are at risk. They are the ones who are going to be losing those jobs which are moving down south of the border. This is just an additional indignity that these women have to suffer.
In closing, I just want to say in support of this motion that the government should be supporting rural Canada through the post office, through support for community development, through support for child care programs, through support for women's programs, and by providing a full range of services and skills training to support the crucial role played by women in all rural communities.

Madam Speaker, I know how committed my hon. friend is to women's issues. I noticed she mentioned on a couple of occasions the social problems which society is witnessing now. They are almost foreboding when you sit down and list them all and wonder if there will ever be solutions. She also spoke about the lack of commitment that we find with the current government in reference to child care services. It seems to go in cycles. I am sure that we will hear from the government again just prior to the next election.
I wonder if my hon. friend sees any correlation, as I do, between the lack of child care services and what constitutes some of our major social problems. We all know that those early years are the years in which some kind of service offered to children has a tremendous impact on their later lives. Does she see a correlation there between the lack of child care services, which are
March 23, 1990

begging, and the social deprivation and social problems which follow from that dearth of services?

Madam Speaker, the hon. member has put it very well. Child care services are an investment in our future. If we do not have those child care services provided, women who are the primarily child care givers in our country have the terrible option of leaving their children at home in order to find the means to support them.
If there is not a national child care scheme, then it is our future that we are jeopardizing. We can either invest in children when they are small or in increasing the number of prisons and mental institutions, for those children who are neglected in their youth are disproportionately the ones who are in our prisons and mental institutions.
That is not overdramatizing the need for a national child care program. The ones who are being neglected are the children of Canada. I would urge the government not to wait for the next election but to act now to institute a national child care program.

Madam Speaker, I would like to compliment my colleague, the member for Saanich-Gulf Islands, for speaking so eloquently of one of our predecessors in the House, Agnes MacPhail, and the work that Agnes did over the years not only for the women throughout Canada but for citizens throughout this country who live in our smaller rural communities.
In passing, my colleague made specific mention of some of the concerns that we have about the direction that Canada Post is taking in eliminating a very needed and necessary service with the post offices in our smaller communities.
My area in the Okanagan-Shuswap has a number of these small communities. I know that the citizens in those areas are most concerned with what they see as an erosion of not only the quality of service that is given by Canada Post but an erosion of the very dynamics and the social fabric of those small communities. Those members who have smaller communities in their ridings would agree with me that the post office is very often a centre of social activity where people come to meet on a regular basis and chit-chat as they pick up their mail.
Supply
The arguments we have been hearing in those communities where the post offices have been closed is that whole nature changes when the post office service has been privatized to a retail outlet. I know in one particular area of my community up in the north Shuswap there is considerable concern now that that has been privatized. Even though the individual is doing the best job that he can in providing a retail service, it has to come secondary to what he is really there for, and that is a retail grocery outlet. For much of the service that this individual provides, there is no payment provided in the contract. Much of the work he is doing on behalf of the community, I might add, is being done without adequate remuneration.
There are a number of other smaller communities in my area such as Lumby, Armstrong and Enderby where notice has been served that retail outlets will also be established. I think it is step one in what will be a phasing out of Canada Post in those communities.
On behalf of those citizens who have spoken to me very clearly, they see it as a real erosion in the quality of life in rural Canada, and particularly in the Okanagan- Shuswap area. Those individuals want to go on record as saying that this erosion of service and the erosion of the lifestyle that they are used must be stopped. We must continue to provide the kind of service that Canada Post has provided to those communities throughout Canada. We want to see that kind of service continued.

Madam Speaker, the comments of my colleague from Okanagan-Shuswap echo a number of other comments regarding Canada Post and the destruction of rural Canada through the government's initiatives. We stand as part of this motion in condemning that action. I know in my riding it is the same story: the ongoing rural post office privatization initiatives are really hurting the rural communities.
The destruction of rural communities is the destruction of the whole history of Canada and the way we want to live. Those people choose to live in small communities for very good reasons. When the services are withdrawn from them they sometimes have no option but to move into the bigger cities and bring with them a whole bunch of social problems. It is a negative dynamic that should be reversed by the Canadian government giving the kind of resources to Canada Post so it can support rural post offices.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Lise Bourgault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, thank you for recognizing me, because I really want to ask my colleague a question. When the special committee formed by the government and chaired by our colleague, the Minister of State for Indian Affairs and Northern Development, travelled across Canada, obviously the matter of child care in rural areas came up. Among other things, rural women have very special needs for child care. At various hearings, for example, farm women told us they have to wait until the children come home from school to go to the bam. They need more flexibility and want the government to provide appropriate measures. They asked for bigger tax credits and larger child care expense deductions.
So I would like to ask the hon. member if she agrees that in the first part of the child care strategy, the government has recognized these needs, especially for farm women. For example, deductible child care expenses were increased by $4,000. We will agree that it is never enough because we would like to do more for farm women. Does the hon. member agree with the government which raised child care expense deductions so that farm women could have services, because farm women do not need public services; they need private services in the community, where children are kept by neighbours, but for that they need receipts and higher child care expense deductions. So does she agree with the government on that?

Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for her question. That is an important initiative of the government, but it certainly falls far short of a national child care scheme. The hon. member is quite right that they need flexibility. We are not talking about large day care centres. We are talking about flexible arrangements so that women who mainly have to make the arrangements for child care have the ability to make them. However, if there are no child care spaces available, there is very little to arrange. When we are seeing the destruction of rural communities there are no neighbours for the women to leave their children with. A kind of danger that exists where children are left alone or left near farm equipment, and every year at harvest
time we hear sad stories where children are injured by farm equipment.
The government should be taking an initiative for a national child care scheme, to provide the dignity of the workplace for the child care workers and the safe environment for children to be cared for.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this is an important motion before the House this afternoon. I would like to make sure the House understands that we consider it so important that I am going to share this time slot with my colleague for Argenteuil-Papineau.
First of all I want to compliment my friend from Prince Albert on the way he has put this motion together, particularly the second clause which refers to the fishery. Quite clearly, he has captured the essence of the problem that we face in the fishery.
He has captured the essence of the process that we as a country must pursue to deal with the problem if we are going to come to terms not only with the economy of Atlantic Canada in particular but also with the very nature of the rural part of this country that has been there so much longer than the rest. He has said that we must assist fishing communities to survive the current crisis and we must ensure proper management of the fishery in the future.
Those are exactly the two principles that are guiding and have guided this government in dealing with this very clear and very obvious crisis that we face. We know, as I think all Canadians know, that there are less fish to be caught and less fish going to be produced. As a result there will be less people there to produce the fish.
The first thing that we must do that is tantamount to any action that we take in dealing with the fishery is to deal with the conservation question. We must make sure that we have fish there that will sustain Atlantic Canadians for as long as Atlantic Canadians want to pursue the fishery.
We must take whatever action is necessary to make sure that the fish stocks, wherever they grow, can be enhanced so that there are fish there to be taken and produced. That must be our concern.
In recognition that clearly we do not have enough knowledge to make those decisions properly all the time,
March 23, 1990

in recognition of the scientific advice particularly as it was applied to the northern cod stock in the area we know as 2J3KL, we appointed a group of eminent people, including scientists from around the world and Canadians who understood the fishery. It was headed by Dr. Les Harris, president of Memorial University. We have asked them to tell us what we must know and do to be able to make better and sounder decisions.
He tells us that the model is right. He tells us that things are not bad but obviously we must do more. We know that from his first report. His second report is coming and the government will be in a position to carry out many of his recommendations. The government will be able to talk to Canadians about what Dr. Harris and his panel will suggest that we do. Those who have a stake in the industry and depend on the fishery primarily in rural Atlantic Canada can say what must be done for the future.
There is no question that those who depend on the fishery the most are those who are telling us in the strongest terms that we must take action to protect the fishery and ensure through conservation measures that there is a cod stock in the future. We know that the effects reach far beyond the fish stock itself. Clearly, we have seen fish plants closing and trawlers tied up. In some areas of my province of Newfoundland we have seen inshore fishermen catch virtually no fish where they and their fathers and their grandfathers have fished for years without any problem.
As always, it is the people and the communities to whom we have to respond, because they are the most important. We can come to terms with the problem of the fish stocks. But we must be able to tell Canadians who depend on the fishery that we will help them.
What we did with the Harris report in Newfoundland and Labrador, we did with Jean-Eudes Hache in Nova Scotia. He looked at the capacity problem and has given us some advice on what we must do.
But how have we dealt with the people to assist them and the communities to survive? We established a cabinet committee under the chairmanship of the right hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs to bring together all the resources of the government to determine what we must do as a government and as a country
Supply
to deal with these problems and what we must have in place for people.
We have approached this in two ways. In the short term, we immediately ensured that a $130 million package was available to those people in those communities that needed it most. Of course, there is unemployment insurance. Community Futures and the Industrial Adjustment Strategy are the two most important components not only of what we need to do to survive but also in terms of what this resolution is demanding of the government. Quite clearly, we are well on the way to achieving what is stated in the resolution.
The IAS is implemented the minute the plant is closed, and is complemented by Community Futures and a number of other programs. The essence of these programs is to respond as a government to the people who know their community and its resources in a way that will provide alternatives, that will create new economic opportunities, that will create different job opportunities, that will give a future perhaps in a whole different industry, perhaps in the same industry but in a different way, to the people of the community, particularly the young people.
We recognize that there are other requirements. We have a special problem in dealing with older workers who have less mobility opportunities and less training opportunities. We have said we are going to enter into a program to help older workers, and that is being undertaken with the provinces. The mobility and the training functions are there. They are important as components to an over-all package as we assist communities to survive the current crisis in the fishery.
Very clearly, we are saying to the people of Atlantic Canada that we will bring together the resources that we have in the federal government, which is about $130 million. As well, the cabinet committee, particularly as a result of a lot of the work that Ken Stein's committee has done, is looking at other ways to help people deal with their future inside the fishery and outside the fishery. We must be able to provide people with new resources as we consider underutilized species, new markets and new technologies. These are matters on which, particularly with the new Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, a great deal of work has been done to ensure that a package is in place and is ready.

March 23, 1990
Supply
About two hours after the new Minister of Fisheries and Oceans was sworn in he said to me that the first thing he wanted to do was consult with the people who could best tell him as the minister what the real problems were and what the real solutions were. Less than 48 hours later, the new Minister of Fisheries and Oceans left for Shippagan in northern New Brunswick to meet the premiers of the four Atlantic provinces, into Prince Edward Island, down to Gaultois, meeting with the workers and the people of Trepassey and Grand Bank and the people of St. John's who have been affected by the close down, as well as the small producers and the unions. Off we went the next day to Lockeport and Canso, in less than 24 hours. That is the sign of a government that is concerned first and foremost about how to assist communities survive this crisis. We recognize there is a crisis and we recognize that action has to be taken.
I congratulate my friend across the way for endorsing the actions that the government has taken to deal with the problems of rural Canada, particularly in the part of the country that means so much to me, frankly, if I can be a little parochial. I am delighted that he has endorsed the two fundamental tenets here; that we have proper management which ensures conservation, and that we assist communities to survive this crisis. That is exactly what we have been doing. That is what we are doing now and that is what we will do in the future.

Madam Speaker, this government has been in power now for five years. If I were going to be cynical about this, I would suggest that if we leave the problem long enough those rural communities are going to disappear and the government will not have to deal with them. That is one way of solving the problem. Just make sure you do not do anything for five or six years and eventually there will be no rural communities and you have no problem.
I say this out of a certain amount of experience. In 1985 the government, both in agriculture and in the fisheries, indicated it was going to put in place a program which would kick in automatically to help these communities survive. It was supposed to help the farmers, fishermen and foresters survive so that they would have in place an insurance structure, if you wish, which would
kick in. That was back in 1985. They were still talking about it in the 1988 election.
The government claims proudly that is acted within 48 hours after the crisis. This motion suggests that we need to put in place a program which is ready to be implemented when the crisis starts. That is the basis under which the planning should have been done. Six years later is too late.
The Minister of Agriculture took a similar approach to the problem as the hon. member. Why does the government not put more of a human face on its decisions on the economy? Why does it not make sure, first of all, that these communities survive before doing a study which is going to find out whether the fish are going to survive, or in the case of agriculture, whether it is going to be worth while to grow more of a particular type of grain? Why does this government not put a more human face on the problems out there?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the 25 or 30 or 50 farmers in my riding are probably very unhappy with me because I have never spoken on agriculture. I have never spoken on agriculture for one very good reason. I do not know a hill of beans about agriculture, but I do know a couple of things about the fishery.
We talk about waiting five years to deal with the problem. From 1986 to 1988, we had the best three years in the fishery that we ever had in this country. The total allowable catch for northern cod was recommended at
295,000	tons two years ago, and we chose in the interest of conservation to set it at 265,000 tons. The problem we faced is that all of a sudden we were told that instead of being 265,000, when they wanted it at 295,000, it should be set at 125,000 tons. As a result we have a problem. That is where the problem is.
I think there is an understanding that provinces have allowed, for instance, virtually doubling the expansion of capacity to respond to rural situations in Canada. We have seen far too many people go into the fishery as an employment option of last resort.
Fishermen are the only self-employed people in this country who can qualify for unemployment insurance. Community Futures which spreads right across Newfoundland is designed specifically to deal with rural problems like this on a regional basis. It has been hugely successful. We are trying to ensure that young Newfoundlanders and Labradorians can get from school to a workplace in a sensible and organized fashion. We are
March 23, 1990

spending $56 million to find out why it does not happen. For the last four years we have had emergency response.
We have had an emergency response which has kicked in every year. We did not have to find the money because we budgeted for it. We knew these problems were going to happen. We had been there ready to deal with them.
Let me say one thing, Madam Speaker. The future of the rural communities in Atlantic Canada is fish and if we want to keep a human face on the coastlines of Newfoundland and Labrador we better have fish looking up at those faces, and as a result we must take fish decisions to protect those people and ensure that they have the future that they so badly want.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Lise Bourgault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Madam Speaker, as you know, it is always stimulating to rise in the House after an eloquent speech like the one we just heard by our colleague from Newfoundland. In fact, whenever people from this province speak in the House, I don't know what it is but they have a way with them that is probably typical of Eastern Canada.
It's the electricity!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
The electricity! Again, Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak in the House today, first of all, to pay tribute to the first woman elected to the House of Commons, Agnes MacPhail. Mrs. MacPhail started her career as a teacher in a country school, and she did not forget her rural roots when she came to Parliament in 1921. She went into politics to represent the farmers in her riding, but it was not long before she expanded her activities to include an interest in women's issues. She was energetic in her defence of women's civil rights. Subsequently, as a member of the Ontario Legislature, she helped bring about the first wage parity legislation in Ontario, passed in 1951.
Many of these and other issues have made enormous progress since Agnes MacPhail sat in the House of Commons. I think she would be proud, Madam Speaker, of the number of women sitting in Parliament today and to see you sitting in the Speaker's chair, as she would be
Supply
proud of the many Canadian women in positions of power and responsibility in all areas of our society.
I believe Agnes MacPhail would be especially happy to see the tremendous progress made by farm women in promoting their legal, social and economic rights.
With their spouses, these women now operate the vast majority, fact 99 per cent, of Canadian farms. Since 1975, the number of women operating farms independently almost tripled in Canada, increasing from 13,000 to
35,000.	Furthermore, 23,000 women are sole owners of their farms in this country.
Officially, women represent 30 per cent of Canada's labour force in the agricultural industry, but this of course does not includes the thousands of Canadian women who combine work on the farm with another job to help support their families.
Women shoulder their share of financing, production and administration on Canada's family farm operations. In other words, they do their share of the work. In 1987, the National Farm Women's Conference found that in this country, women carried out 49 per cent of the farm chores and 97 per cent of the home making chores. We should not overlook that these same women are often involved in a career away from the farm. These women have guts.
In 1986, the Census of agriculture revealed that in this country, one third of all women farmers have a university or college education and currently use their special training and knowledge in the management of the farm or in the profession they are engaged in away from the farm. Madam Speaker, a great many of them use them in both.
Today, the Federal Government is more aware than ever of the enormous contribution women make to agriculture in this country. We know their contribution as farm managers, homemakers and family providers. We support women in their efforts to ensure a certain quality of life in the farm community and I know that it is not always easy.
One of the major areas in which our Government is striving to help women farmers is through the development of strategies with a view to harmonizing professional and family responsibilities.

March 23, 1990
Supply
The Government's policies in this area should clearly recognize the unique character of the work and family obligations which is particular to family farms. They should take it into account.
During the First Ministers' Conference which was held last November, the Federal, Provincial and Territorial ministers responsible for the status of women tabled a report describing the strategies which each government intends to implement in an effort to promote the integration of professional and family responsibilities.
Our purpose is to support women and men in their work environment, while helping them to assume then-responsibilities as parents and as breadwinners.
At that First Ministers' Conference the Canadian ministers responsible for the status of women tabled various reports describing some of the major government projects undertaken in recent years to ensure that, in education and training, women throughout Canada would be considered equal and have access to all facilities.
Not unlike Canadians in other economic sectors, women involved in farming know that training is essential if they are to keep up with the ever increasing pace of technological changes. These women never miss an opportunity to express their views on this issue.
After all, it was back in 1985 at the second national conference of women in agriculture that for the first time somebody suggested that women ought to have readier access to training.
At the present time, representatives of the Canadian Council of Education for Women Farmers and Employment and Immigration Canada officials are working together to develop strategies designed to encourage more women farmers to enrol in training programs.
I think the government, women farmers and their organizations must contuinue to communicate and exchange views on issues such as training, working conditions and family life.
Mr. Speaker, women farmers in my riding are very well organized and I meet with them on a regular basis. Not so long ago the issue of child care in rural areas came up. As I pointed out in a question to an NDP colleague,
women farmers have special needs concerning child care, and they want the government to show some flexibility in the implementation of national programs so that they will be able to have someone to look after their children when it becomes necessary. Farm women have to go to the bam when the children come home from school. They often live in outlying areas and their particular needs cannot be compared with those of city women. It is therefore imperative that the government take their needs into account in its national child care strategy. We have listened carefully to what these women told us during hearings of the Special Committee on Child Care. The government has responded, in the first phase of its national child care strategy, by, among other things, doubling the amount of eligible expenses to $4,000 and by increasing the child tax credit by $200 per child for youngsters.
Mr. Speaker, I can assure the farmers of my constituency of Argenteuil-Papineau, a very agricultural and prosperous riding, that I am following with interest the development of agriculture and that I do not hesitate to defend their interests whenever the opportunity arises and that I will continue to do so as long as I am sitting in this House.

Mr. Speaker, given the time of day, I would like to address two issues in the last minutes of this very interesting debate on rural life in Canada.
In particular, I would like to deal with issues which concern western Canadians. One issue deals with the role of the western diversification fund in our economy. We heard earlier today an eloquent defence of government activities by the Minister of Agriculture, and he spoke in some detail about what the government says it is doing to help western farmers.
The reality is that the western Canadian economy needs much more than this government can provide and the fact that it is cash-short is as much a result of the government's own strategy and its own programming as it is with anything else. The fact that the government is not able to contribute sufficiently to the western economy is a product of the government's own reasoning and its own lack of imagination in helping westerners.
March 23, 1990

In particular, one of the most controversial aspects of its program has been the western diversification fund. Since its inception, the Progressive Conservative government has long trumpeted the Department of Western Economic Diversification as the answer to western Canada's economic woes. The program was announced previous to the 1988 general election with a great deal of fanfare. It would consolidate two programs; the western diversification fund which was announced in August
1987,	and the ERDA program which was started by the Liberals earlier in the 1980s.
The total value of these programs was to exceed $2.8 billion. At that time, the Prime Minister stated that the ERDA program would remain intact and the western diversification fund would be created out of new money. There was a great deal of promise from 1987 through
1988,	coincidentally just before the election, as to what the government would do to help out western Canadians. The reality is that the western diversification programming has failed to live up to its promises. Instead of pumping much needed capital into western Canada, it continued to fall short of its publicly stated goals.
For example, in the eight months before the 1988 election western diversification approved over $400 million in projects. In the fiscal year following the election, the government forecast that it would only spend $136.8 million to fulfil these commitments. Last year, the minister responsible for western diversification assured us that everything was on track and that $253 million would be spent. Today, we find that he is only able to fulfil 54 per cent of his commitment.
In Part III of the estimates for the fiscal year we find that he has promised another $252 million. What will be in the budget next year?
Because these statistics are so important, I want to read them into the record as the Minister of Agriculture was so fond of doing during his presentation, so that the Canadian people begin to appreciate what the government has been doing in each year.
In 1987-88, it estimated that it would spend $98.87 million. It actually spent $47,057 million, or 47 per cent of what it estimated. The importance of this is to understand the accumulation of the lack of funds actual-
Supply
ly being put in western Canada as a result of the decisions being made by the federal government.
The next year, 1988-89, the election year, the government promised $293,427,000. After the election it spent $75,300,000, or 25 per cent of the estimated amount. In 1989-90, the minister said in the House: "This year, I am going to spend $252,999,000." We find out now he spent $136 million, or 54 per cent of his target.
This year he says he is going to spend $251 million and we do not know when he is going to do it. The point is that the accumulated estimated amount is about $850 million. The real figure is about $250 million.
We find that the government is shortchanging western Canada. It then has the nerve to turn around and parade all these statistics about how it is helping the farmer. It is failing to help the farmer. It is failing to help diversify the economy in western Canada, and the two ministers responsible for that are the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister for Western Diversification.
I would also like to address very briefly a second issue that is hitting home in western Canada, and that is the changes in the postal rates. The Union of Manitoba Municipalities has kindly brought it to the attention of the government and to members of the opposition that the hike in postal fees is going to have a serious negative effect on daily newspapers.
In Manitoba, for example, The Brandon Sun has been adversely affected by this increase. That paper will have to increase its fees for subscribers who receive then-paper via Canada Post from $114 to $220. The paper is trying to make alternative arrangements for trucking the papers to drop-off points. There will be a certain number which must be mailed out of province, for example.
The circulation manager points out that Canada Post only gave him two days' notice for this change. This is a blow against newspapers, an important communication link for rural areas and it comes at a very bad time. It seemed like another blow against rural areas by Canada Post.
We have heard a lot of discussion in the House in the last few months about the decline in the quality of life in western Canada. There are two components of that, I think. One is a diversification of the economy and the

March 23, 1990
Supply
second is a communications strategy involving Canada Post.
Without the ability to communicate, without the ability to finance interesting projects, western Canada is doomed for a bleak future. I think that that can be directly attributed to the lack of understanding of this government which is a great irony because it spent years in opposition saying that it was the only party that understood western Canada. Yet, when given the opportunity to govern fairly for western Canadians, it has failed miserably.
The only route left for western Canadians to regain their future is to defeat this government and to put in others who understand them, namely, this party.

Mr. Speaker, my Liberal colleague from Winnipeg North Centre brings forth some very interesting arguments regarding the problems with western diversification funding and other regional development funding programs for western Canada. His point is well taken that the funding that was supposed to have been funnelled through such kinds of regional development programs has in fact fallen drastically short of its mark.
Both the western diversification program and the ERDA programs were developed in order to funnel economic development priorities into provinces in the west. For example, we now see in British Columbia, at the end of this month, only a matter of a few days away, the cancellation of a $300 million five-year Forestry Resource Development Agreement that has gone on since 1985. That agreement is now to be terminated with no guarantees that there will be any other funding. The only hint of funding that we see at this point is about $30 million to $40 million to be funnelled in for forestry through western diversification.
We have seen a significant cut in the federal commitment to reforestation initiatives in British Columbia. There is no question that with that reduction in funding for forestry in British Columbia alone, as well as the many other provinces where those agreements are now coming to a close or have already been terminated, we see a significant loss of jobs in the forestry industry in the silviculture programs and replanting. An entire industry infrastructure has been built up around the FRDA
agreements. Now that infrastructure will begin to fall apart with the government essentially knee-capping the funds that are required for forestry development.
In one of the other economic sectors, the Tourism Industry Development Subsidiary Agreements are now also being terminated. The word we get from the Minister of State for Tourism is that those will not be renewed. We are seeing a retraction of the government's commitment to regional development through the kneecapping of funding in these programs.
I certainly concur with my colleague from the Winnipeg area that these programs are conceptually of great value. Yet, politically speaking, there simply has not been the kind of political or economic initiative supplied to these programs by this government to really make them work.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the member from British Columbia for reminding me about the forestry industry which I should have addressed more directly in my comments. It is impossible to understand the failure to renew an adequate agreement in forestry. Those who know the industry will know that it is the biggest employer in Canada when you include direct and indirect employment figures. It is the economic backbone of British Columbia. Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba are all trying to develop more aggressive forestry programs. At the very moment that the west is finding a way to broaden its economic base, the federal government walks out on it. That is totally indefensible and totally incomprehensible.
The list of ERDA agreements that are valuable to the west is endless. It would be easier for the government to tell us what it is continuing than for me to list what it is discontinuing.
The fact that the communications agreement is ending in Manitoba in 10 days and putting the motion picture industry there in total disarray is another example of the callousness of this government.

Mr. Speaker, to conclude the debate before us today, I would like to spend the remaining few minutes speaking about the other major initiative in this motion, and that is the fishery.
March 23, 1990

There is a crisis in the fishing industry, there are communities closing down, and there is a call by members of Parliament to put money into these communities to help them readjust. I contend that perhaps the greatest crisis facing the industry in eastern Canada is the crisis of having a government that is afraid to stop the cause of the problem in the fishery today.
I would like to refer to the facts concerning the fishery. We have, all along the coast of Canada, a 200-mile zone. It is 200 nautical miles, really, that is about 240 or 250 land miles. Within that zone Canada manages our fishing resource and has since 1977 when we declared the 200-mile zone like every other country in the world.
Let us look at the allocations for this year, at who is allowed to catch the fish inside of our 200-mile zone. Under the NAFO agreements, that is an international organization which manages fish stocks that come within the 200-mile zone and outside the 200-mile zone, the allocations are 310,500 metric tons to countries like Bulgaria, Cuba, the EEC, East Germany, Japan, Norway, Poland, U.S.S.R., and others. Then we have Canada's managed fish stocks. Under that we see that the total foreign allocations are 182,962 for 1990. Add both of them up and you get a figure of 493,462 metric tons.
What is the Canadian allocation? The Canadian allocation is, and I quote from the same document, 612,265 metric tons. So Canada is able to fish 600,000 metric tons, foreign nations are able to fish 500,000 metric tons, and the seals eating about two million metric tons. So between the foreigners and the seals we have a problem in the fishery in eastern Canada.
Here we are wondering what to do about the communities that are closing. Today MPs in their offices are taking calls from around the coastline. A gentleman called my office this morning from another person's riding and said: "Look, I cannot fish capelin this year. I am not allowed". He is not allowed to fish capelin this year because of a restricted entry regulation which was passed last year which said that you must be the skipper of a crew of at least three people and your boat has to be a certain size. These gentlemen, who have been fulltime fishermen all their lives, are not allowed to fish capelin this year.

Yet we see increases in capelin allocations to Cuba, increases to Japan, increases to Norway, increases to Poland, increases to the U.S.S.R., and restrictions on Canadians.
What is the problem in the east coast fishery today? Ask a fisherman, Mr. Speaker, and he will say: "We don't want money from the Government of Canada, we want the right to be able to fish".
In regard to all of this that is going on, I will read something into the record. For all of the fishermen of eastern Canada, here it is. Listen now, because you are going to hear it straight from the Government of Canada, the Government of the Soviet Union and all of those foreign nations. This is a letter to the Canadian government dated just four weeks ago.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext: Table it.

I will table it, indeed I will. Just listen to this. I quote the Soviet side:
- taking into account the desire of both sides to preserve stability, considers that the total U.S.S.R. allocations for 1990 in the Canadian zone should not be less than the allocation for 1989.
"To preserve stability". What does that threat mean from the Soviet Union? Not only from them, but from Cuba, Poland, Norway, East Germany, Bulgaria. What do they mean?
Then we get the response. This was written four weeks ago to the Government of Canada. The answer sent back from the Government of Canada says, pursuant to our agreement on mutual fisheries relations, the following initial quotas are given.
And then we see it: cod, redfish, Greenland halibut, grenadier, silver hake, Argentine, squid. Here they are, all in the allocations. Both sides agree.
The letter continues:
The Canadian side confirms its intention to cooperate further with
the Soviet side.
So there it is. While Canadian fishermen cannot fish, while Canadian fishermen are being cut back, foreign nations write to this government and say in order to "preserve stability". What are they going to do; invade us? In order to preserve stability we want the same quotas we had last year, while Canadians have been cut back, while our fish plants are closing, while our fisher-

Here we have it. I am tabling it so all of these Tories can read it so they will know what is going on behind the scenes. Or perhaps they do know what is going on behind the scenes.
As if that was not enough, in this letter it says, and I quote again this letter that I would like the government members to read. It states here:
The Soviet side undertakes to finalize an exchange with the
Canadian side-(involving) 2 +3K capelin-
Now that may not mean very much to some people sitting in their fancy offices, but if you were to tell a fisherman that you are about to negotiate again with the Soviet Union, Cuba, East Germany and Bulgaria to give them more capelin, which is what codfish eat-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext: Male capelin.

The hon. gentleman says "male capelin". A codfish does not ask whether it is male or female. He will eat it no matter what it is.
Here we are today in the concluding moments of debate on a resolution asking the Government of Canada to properly manage the fisheries of our nation. We are asking for money. And here is the Canadian Government giving just as much to the foreigners as it gives to Canadians. It is afraid to take the initial steps to guarantee our fishermen their same quotas.
The Department of External Affairs runs the Department of Fisheries in this nation. The fishermen of Canada are saying to the Government of Canada: "All we want is the chance to fish. We do not want to be retrained with these great agreements that the Government of Canada is about to announce. We want to fish. That is what we have done all of our lives. You are today preventing us from fishing. You are today assigning to foreign nations exactly the same fish that we want."
